items.title: alibaba/open-code-review
items.content:
Secure, fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.

What is Open Code Review?

Open Code Review is an AI-powered code review CLI tool. It originated as Alibaba Group's internal official AI code review assistant — over the past two years, it has served tens of thousands of developers and identified millions of code defects. After thorough validation at massive scale, we incubated it into an open source project for the community. Simply configure a model endpoint to get started.

It reads Git diffs, sends changed files to a configurable LLM via an agent with tool-use capabilities, and generates structured review comments with line-level precision. The agent can read full file contents, search the codebase, inspect other changed files for context, and produce deep reviews — not just surface-level diff feedback. Beyond diff review, reviews entire files for auditing unfamiliar codebases or directories that have no meaningful diff.

Compared to general-purpose agents (Claude Code), Open Code Review achieves significantly higher and with the same underlying model, while consuming only and completing reviews faster. Note that its Recall is lower than general-purpose agents — a deliberate trade-off favoring precision over noise.

A real-world code review benchmark built from popular open-source repositories, real Pull Requests, and programming languages — cross-validated by 80+ senior engineers ( annotated ground-truth issues).

Harmonic mean of precision and recallBest single number for overall review quality
Proportion of reported issues that are real defectsHigher = fewer false alarms to triage
Proportion of real defects that are foundHigher = fewer issues slip through review
Wall-clock time per reviewMatters for CI pipeline latency
Total tokens consumed per reviewDirectly impacts API cost

The Problem with General-Purpose Agents

If you've used general-purpose agents like Claude Code with Skills for code review, you've likely encountered these pain points:

  • — On larger changesets, agents tend to "cut corners," selectively reviewing only some files and missing others.
  • — Reported issues frequently don't match the actual code location, with line numbers or file references drifting off target.
  • — Natural-language-driven Skills are hard to debug, and review quality fluctuates significantly with minor prompt variations.

The root cause: a purely language-driven architecture lacks hard constraints on the review process.

Core Design: Deterministic Engineering × Agent Hybrid

Open Code Review's core philosophy is to combine deterministic engineering with an agent, each handling what it does best.

Deterministic Engineering — Hard Constraints

For review steps that , engineering logic — not the language model — guarantees correctness:

  • — Determines exactly which files need review and which should be filtered, ensuring no important change is missed.
  • — Groups related files into a single review unit (e.g., and are bundled together). Each bundle runs as a sub-agent with isolated context — a divide-and-conquer strategy that stays stable on very large changesets and naturally supports concurrent review.
  • Fine-grained rule matching — Matches review rules to each file's characteristics, keeping the model's attention sharply focused and eliminating information noise at the source. Compared to purely language-driven rule guidance, template-engine-based rule matching is more stable and predictable.
  • External positioning and reflection modules — Independent comment-positioning and comment-reflection modules systematically improve both the location accuracy and content accuracy of AI feedback.

Agent — Dynamic Decision-Making

The agent's strengths are concentrated where they matter most — dynamic decisions and dynamic context retrieval:

  • — Prompt templates deeply optimized for code review, improving effectiveness while reducing token consumption.
  • — Distilled from deep analysis of tool-call traces in large-scale production data — including call frequency distributions, per-tool repetition rates, and the impact of new tools on the overall call chain — resulting in a purpose-built toolset that is more stable and predictable for code review than a generic agent toolkit.
  • — Open Code Review relies on Git for diff generation, code search, and repository operations.
npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review

After installation, the command is available globally.

For other installation methods (install script, GitHub Release binary, from source), see Installation.

You must configure an LLM before reviewing code, unless you use Delegation Mode.

  • , the command, and the skill use OCR's own provider configuration, not your Claude Code Team/Pro subscription login. Authentication requirements depend on the provider; see Configuration.
  • The host agent calls the model: the /open-code-review:delegate-review command and the open-code-review-delegate skill use the host agent's configured model and authentication. No separate LLM configuration or credentials are needed in OCR. See the Claude Code install steps.
ocr config provider          # Select a built-in provider or add a custom one
ocr config model             # Pick a model for the active provider

The interactive UI guides you through provider selection, API key entry, and model configuration, then automatically tests connectivity.

For CLI setup, environment variables, custom providers, and other advanced configuration, see Configuration.

cd your-project

# Workspace mode — review all staged, unstaged, and untracked changes
ocr review

# Branch range — reviews feature-branch's changes since it diverged from main (merge-base mode)
ocr review --from main --to feature-branch

# Single commit
ocr review --commit abc123

# Resume an interrupted range or commit review
ocr session list
ocr review --from main --to feature-branch --resume <session-id>

# Full-file scan — review whole files instead of a diff (no git history needed)
ocr scan                          # scan the entire repository
ocr scan --path internal/agent    # scan a directory or specific files
ocr scan --resume <session-id>   # resume an interrupted full-file scan

# Save results to a file (recommended for AI host agents)
ocr review --format json --output result.json

# Delegation mode — let your AI coding agent perform the review itself
# OCR handles file selection and rule resolution; no LLM configuration needed
ocr delegate preview
ocr delegate rule src/main.go src/handler.go
  • Review Rules — customize review rules with path filtering and targeting
  • MCP Server — extend the review agent with external tools
  • Coding Agent Integrations — choose the platform you use
    • Claude Code — install a plugin with review slash commands
    • Codex — install a plugin with callable review skills
    • Cursor — install a plugin with portable review skills
    • Kimi Code — install a plugin with review slash commands and skills
    • OpenCode — install native review tools and slash commands
    • QCA Forward — run delegation mode with the QCA host model and a ready-to-publish template
  • Review Execution Modes — after integration, choose which LLM performs the review
  • Session Viewer — browse and replay review sessions in browser, mark comments as fixed or ignored and hide them while you work through the findings
  • Telemetry — OpenTelemetry integration for observability
  • FAQ — common questions and troubleshooting

This project exists thanks to all the people who contribute. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup, coding guidelines, and how to submit pull requests.

items.title: ggml-org/llama.cpp
items.content:
A few options to get installed on your machine:

# curl
curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh

# powershell
irm https://llama.app/install.ps1 | iex

# Download and run a model directly from Hugging Face
llama cli -hf ggml-org/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF

# Launch OpenAI-compatible API server
llama serve -hf ggml-org/Qwen3.5-0.8B-GGUF

The main goal of is to enable LLM (and VLM) inference with minimal setup and state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of hardware - locally and in the cloud.

  • Plain C/C++ implementation without any dependencies
  • Apple silicon is a first-class citizen - optimized via ARM NEON, Accelerate and Metal frameworks
  • AVX, AVX2, AVX512 and AMX support for x86 architectures
  • RVV, ZVFH, ZFH, ZICBOP and ZIHINTPAUSE support for RISC-V architectures
  • 1.5-bit, 2-bit, 3-bit, 4-bit, 5-bit, 6-bit, and 8-bit integer quantization for faster inference and reduced memory use
  • Custom CUDA kernels for running LLMs on NVIDIA GPUs (support for AMD GPUs via HIP and Moore Threads GPUs via MUSA)
  • Vulkan and SYCL backend support
  • CPU+GPU hybrid inference to partially accelerate models larger than the total VRAM capacity

The project is build on top of the ggml library.

  • Contributors can open PRs
  • Collaborators will be invited based on contributions
  • Maintainers can push to branches in the repo and merge PRs into the branch
  • Any help with managing issues, PRs and projects is very appreciated!

  • nlohmann/json - Single-header JSON library, used by various tools/examples - MIT License
  • mackron/miniaudio - Single-header audio format decoder, used by multimodal subsystem - Public domain

items.content:
Node.js JavaScript runtime ✨🐢🚀✨

Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment.

Contributors are expected to act in a collaborative manner to move the project forward. We encourage the constructive exchange of contrary opinions and compromise. The TSC reserves the right to limit or block contributors who repeatedly act in ways that discourage, exhaust, or otherwise negatively affect other participants.

  • : Under active development where semver-major changes are allowed. Each October, a new release line (for example, Node.js 27) branches off and receives Alpha releases (for example, ) for 6 months, then are promoted to Current (see below) each April. Alpha releases are signed, tagged, and tested through CITGM, but their API and ABI may change between releases. They are intended for library authors and CI pipelines, not for production use.
  • : Under active development, no semver-major changes allowed. Node.js releases a new major version once a year, in April. Releases stay Current for 6 months, then convert to LTS (see below) each October. Their ABI may change between releases. They are intended for library authors and CI pipelines, not for production use.
  • : Releases under Long Term Support, with a focus on stability and security. Only changes that have been on Alpha or Current release for two weeks can be backported to a typical LTS release. Every major version becomes an LTS release, and receives 30 months of LTS support, for a total of 36 months from its first Current release to End-of-Life. LTS release lines have alphabetically-ordered code names, beginning with Node.js 4 Argon.
  • : Code from the branch built every 24-hours when there are changes. Unlike Alpha releases, nightly builds are automated and untested. Use with caution.

Release lines up to and including Node.js 26 follow the previous schedule, where a new major version was released every 6 months and only even-numbered major versions became LTS. See the Node.js release schedule announcement for details.

The latest directory is an alias for the latest Current release. The latest- directory is an alias for the latest release from an LTS line. For example, the latest-hydrogen directory contains the latest Hydrogen (Node.js 18) release.

Each directory and filename includes the version (e.g., ), followed by the UTC date (e.g., for April 24, 2024), and the short commit SHA of the HEAD of the release (e.g., ). For instance, a full directory name might look like v22.0.0-nightly20240424ddd0a9e494.

Download directories contain a file with SHA checksums for the files and the releaser PGP signature.

You can get a trusted keyring from nodejs/release-keys, e.g. using :

curl -fsLo "/path/to/nodejs-keyring.kbx" "https://github.com/nodejs/release-keys/raw/HEAD/gpg/pubring.kbx"

Alternatively, you can import the releaser keys in your default keyring, see Release keys for commands on how to do that.

Then, you can verify the files you've downloaded locally (if you're using your default keyring, pass --keyring="${GNUPGHOME:-~/.gnupg}/pubring.kbx"):

curl -fsO "https://nodejs.org/dist/${VERSION}/SHASUMS256.txt.asc" \
&& gpgv --keyring="/path/to/nodejs-keyring.kbx" --output SHASUMS256.txt < SHASUMS256.txt.asc \
&& shasum --check SHASUMS256.txt --ignore-missing

See BUILDING.md for instructions on how to build Node.js from source and a list of supported platforms.

For information on reporting security vulnerabilities in Node.js, see SECURITY.md.

Current project team members

For information about the governance of the Node.js project, see GOVERNANCE.md.

TSC (Technical Steering Committee)

Triagers follow the Triage Guide when responding to new issues.

Primary GPG keys for Node.js Releasers (some Releasers sign with subkeys):

gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys 5BE8A3F6C8A5C01D106C0AD820B1A390B168D356 # Antoine du Hamel
gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys DD792F5973C6DE52C432CBDAC77ABFA00DDBF2B7 # Juan José Arboleda
gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys CC68F5A3106FF448322E48ED27F5E38D5B0A215F # Marco Ippolito
gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys 890C08DB8579162FEE0DF9DB8BEAB4DFCF555EF4 # Rafael Gonzaga
gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys C82FA3AE1CBEDC6BE46B9360C43CEC45C17AB93C # Richard Lau
gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys 108F52B48DB57BB0CC439B2997B01419BD92F80A # Ruy Adorno
gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys 655F3B5C1FB3FA8D1A0CA6BDE4A7D232B936D2FD # Stewart X Addison
gpg --keyserver hkps://keys.openpgp.org --recv-keys A363A499291CBBC940DD62E41F10027AF002F8B0 # Ulises Gascón

Security release stewards

When possible, the commitment to take slots in the security release steward rotation is made by companies in order to ensure individuals who act as security stewards have the support and recognition from their employer to be able to prioritize security releases. Security release stewards manage security releases on a rotation basis as outlined in the security release process.

This project also depends on external libraries that may use different open-source licenses. For a complete list of included licenses, please see the LICENSE file.

If you are contributing documentation or source changes, please ensure your additions comply with the project’s license guidelines.

items.title: ashhart/TensorFold
items.content:
LLM Inference Engine for Metal, CUDA and Vulkan.

TensorFold serves language models from a Zig binary on Apple Silicon and NVIDIA GPUs. The engine reads checkpoints, tokenizes requests and runs Metal or CUDA kernels directly. Serving needs no Python or MLX installation.

Building with a coding agent? Have it load the contributor skill before it writes any code.

Install or upgrade ATC to 0.9.4 or later, then run from an updated TensorFold clone:

npm install -g github:ashhart/ATC
atc check ISSUE --json
atc claim ISSUE --json

Replace with the issue number and claim only after a complete check says the work is free. TensorFold enables automatic public check-ins: a successful new claim starts an anonymous session on the radar and returns its number. Keep that number instead of starting a duplicate session. For work already yours, start a session with . Add to or only if you want your verified GitHub name shown; keeps a new session on your machine. The board shows the issue, activity state and last check-in; GitHub still associates the verification comment with its author. Check that is ; means the public update failed even if the local claim or session succeeded.

Pulse only while the agent is working, before its five-minute check-in expires:

atc pulse ISSUE SESSION working --json
atc who path/to/file --json
atc overlap --json
atc land ISSUE SESSION --json
atc release ISSUE --json

Use or when appropriate, land the session when it stops, and resolve overlaps before opening a pull request. Before opening a pull request, have the agent run the pull request skill; agents that support skills can install it as .

Start with Qwen3.5-2B, the small 4-bit checkpoint checked on Metal and a GB10. The commands below download its pinned revision, then serve it as . Model weights have their own licenses. Reviewing or benchmarking TensorFold? Evaluating TensorFold covers pinning, signature checks, a container and the tests that need no GPU.

Install with Homebrew, then start the server:

brew install ashhart/tensorfold/tensorfold
tensorfold pull mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit@93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3
tensorfold serve mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit --name local-model --context 8192 --no-thinking

Use the release archive for your CPU: on a GB10, on an x86_64 host. It needs glibc 2.28 or newer and NVIDIA driver R580 or newer (CUDA 13.0), providing . Keep the archive's directories together. Its kernels are built with CUDA 13, so TensorFold refuses an older driver at startup; shows the installed one. See the CUDA runbook for runtime libraries and supported GPUs.

V=1.2.7
case "$(uname -m)" in
  aarch64|arm64) PLATFORM=linux-aarch64 ;;
  x86_64) PLATFORM=linux-x86_64 ;;
  *) echo 'No release archive for this CPU' >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
curl -fLO "https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/releases/download/v$V/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
curl -fLO "https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/releases/download/v$V/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256"
sha256sum -c "tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz.sha256"
tar -xzf "tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM.tar.gz"
export PATH="$PWD/tensorfold-$V-$PLATFORM/bin:$PATH"
tensorfold() { command tensorfold-native "$@"; }
tensorfold pull mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit@93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3
tensorfold serve mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit --name local-model --context 8192 --no-thinking

Leave the server running. In another terminal, on either platform:

curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"local-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello in one sentence."}],"max_tokens":128,"temperature":0}'

The API also serves completions, Responses and Anthropic Messages. lists the served name. On Windows with an NVIDIA GPU, follow the native Windows build guide. Use , tensorfold capabilities --json and tensorfold serve REPO --help to inspect your binary. You can also serve a complete local checkpoint directory or an existing Hugging Face cache.

opens TensorFold Web, a small local web app for picking, running and chatting with models. If it needs installing, an interactive release binary offers to install its matching version with after you say yes. See the web launcher for manual installation and unattended use.

caps active requests at N; extra requests wait for a free slot. Omitting the flag uses , which asks for up to eight streams as memory and the engine allow. An explicit number is refused if the engine cannot fit that many streams. Read the engine's startup capacity line, such as on CUDA, for the count it accepted. With API authentication off, reports as active plus waiting requests and as the queued count. For example, 8 connections with 4 waiting means 4 active requests. Completing or cancelling an active request frees its slot; cancelling a waiting request removes it from the queue.

The TensorFold desktop workspace bundles the local engine, model downloads, hardware recommendations, live generation metrics, coding workers and document editing. Download the Apple-silicon beta 9 DMG, or build from . The desktop app launches the bundled executable directly. Mobile clients in remain preview software.

TensorFold Starlight (enterprise)

TensorFold Starlight gives an organisation one governed OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoint for a fleet of TensorFold engines on Macs, Linux GPU servers and Windows machines. It signs people in through the organisation's identity provider (OIDC or SAML, with SCIM provisioning), decides who may use which model and where it runs, places and supervises models on nodes, and accounts for every token. It runs fully offline, or brokers approved frontier providers under the same identity, policy and budgets; the install guide covers Docker, Kubernetes and Linux services. Starlight lives in its own repository, ashhart/tf-starlight: it pins the TensorFold release it is tested with and checks every flag its nodes pass to against that release in CI. Starlight is new: the gates that still need real GPU clusters or identity-provider tenants are listed in its qualification notes.

Living Weights (experimental)

Living Weights teaches a running model new facts in its own weights. Start a Nemotron 3.5 Lightning server with and tell it something: each fact that passes the lesson's checks is written into the checkpoint folder's files. It is experimental: related facts can disturb each other, recall drops past a few dozen facts and with thinking on, and learned facts cost some decode speed on a Mac. Known issues has the details.

tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit
hub="${HF_HUB_CACHE:-${HF_HOME:-$HOME/.cache/huggingface}/hub}/models--TensorFold--NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit"
src="$hub/snapshots/$(cat "$hub/refs/main")"
mkdir -p ~/models && cp -RL "$src" ~/models/nemotron-living   # always teach a copy
(umask 077; openssl rand -hex 24 > ~/models/slide-key)        # --slide starts only with a key
tensorfold serve ~/models/nemotron-living --slide --api-key-file ~/models/slide-key

Leave that server running and send a lesson from another terminal:

curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/slide/learn -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/models/slide-key)" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"text": "I like blue."}'

Send it a document instead and it finds the facts in it and learns them one by one. Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/slide to watch in 3D: the facts, the neurons each one took in the model's layers, the shard files that hold them, and the lesson running now.

Learning runs on Apple-silicon Macs and on an NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark), and a folder that learned on one serves on the other. On an APFS volume, makes a clone that shares the original's data until lessons change it. It rewrites the folder's files: before the first lesson the server keeps the originals in a hidden snapshot, and tensorfold slide rollback ~/models/nemotron-living puts them back, undoing every lesson. The Living Weights guide covers the key, teaching files and web pages, omp's command, the 3D view, undoing lessons, and what to expect.

These are the native release's serving paths. A recipe may also describe the older Python 0.6.6 engine; use its native section and the current changes together. Hardware below records the documented scope, not an unmeasured minimum. Context, parallel requests, prompt caches and drafters need memory beyond the weights. reports the checkpoint's memory floor. Where no RAM capacity is published, inspect that floor before serving a large checkpoint. CUDA release images include sm_80, sm_86, sm_120 and sm_121. The A100 (sm_80) has kernel-check evidence (#846), but no served checkpoint on record, so it is not model-qualified. Nemotron and dense Qwen have NVFP4/FP8 fallback code for sm_80 to sm_89 (#901, #1470); no such model run on sm_80 to sm_89 is recorded.

Run a table command after installation. On a Linux archive installation, use the shell function from Quick start. pins a pull; serve the repository name without the revision after pulling it. Conversions are explicitly marked: their upstream weights need the linked conversion before native serving.

Use the local checkpoint.Native HIP; AMD R9700 () checked, one GPU.Native OCR recipe; full model-card demo matches HF tokens. Native CUDA serves text prompts only (CUDA recipe). No video, MTP head, or Metal qualification.
tensorfold pull mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-MLX-4bit@93760be4f1f69842a46bc13dbdc0f19e291392a3One Mac (M5 Max checked), or one GB10; no RAM minimum published.
tensorfold pull TensorFold/Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bittensorfold pull z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2One Mac (M5 Max/M3 Ultra), or one GB10; a 32 GB Mac needs raised (the startup refusal names the value).27B. Add --drafter z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2; without it decoding is plain.
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B, MLX 4-bittensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bitOne Mac (M1-M5), or one GB10; also checked on RTX 3090 / RTX PRO 6000.
Lightning, mixed oQ4 / oQ6 / oQ8tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-oQ4tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-oQ6tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-oQ8
tensorfold pull nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4One GB10 checked. Non-cluster fallback code exists for sm_80 to sm_89; no NVFP4/FP8 serving run is recorded on sm_80.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B, NVFP4tensorfold pull nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4@82d93699acd3be9e4617c53360fe5b3f5dbeb1b3One or two GB10s; weights 70.8 GiB, 73.2 GiB with vision on one.
Qwen3.8 Flash Next, MLX 6-bittensorfold pull TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-6bit-MTPOne M5 Ultra checked; RAM minimum not published.
Qwen3.8 Flash Next, MLX 4-bittensorfold pull TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTPOne GB10; 73.3 GiB uploaded, plus mapped tables and caches. Metal has a native 4-bit path too (M3 Ultra checked).Native CUDA. NVFP4/two-local-rank and vision paths are experimental. Metal's shared-session limits are in known issues.
tensorfold pull TensorFold/GLM-5.3-Flash-MLX-4bit-MTPTwo M5 Ultras; single-Mac native serving is not qualified.
tensorfold pull Mia-AiLab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-TR3-4bpwTwo CUDA ranks; the release checks the two-GB10 setup.
tensorfold pull nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4@423acf37583782c51c142d145aef733d72943d93Two GB10s at TP=2: @Bizuayeu loaded the whole checkpoint on 1.1.0 in 302.1 s and served it.Native CUDA; contributed run: one token hash per prompt across three runs and a passphrase found in 199,307 tokens; scored prompts and more than two ranks were not covered.
tensorfold pull nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local@76348ddb2be2e35e39ecfc00e75dc07703f4f3d5Two GB10s at TP=2, or three at TP=3 over a ring of direct links: @Bizuayeu loaded it as stored and served it at both sizes. 165.3 GiB of weights, 13% less than NVFP4's.Native CUDA, in 1.1.5 (#1050). NVIDIA's mixed-precision checkpoint: NVFP4 routed experts, FP8 for most of the rest. As close to BF16 as NVFP4 at its smaller size (receipt).
tensorfold pull Bizuayeu/GLM-5.3-Flash-XSFP4@88736f916f8939607fde8a4b881dcae749f7551dTwo GB10s at TP=2, or three at TP=3 over a ring of direct links: @Bizuayeu served it at both sizes. 165.7 GiB of weights.Native CUDA, in 1.1.5 through FP4-Local's path. FP4-Local with its routed experts refitted from the BF16 weights and a smoothing folded in, on the same kernels. Closer to BF16 than FP4-Local and NVFP4 by all three measures in its card.
GLM-5.3-Flash, Jammed XSFP4tensorfold pull Bizuayeu/GLM-5.3-Flash-Jammed-XSFP4@0a22bb46ecef3d0f5f96e41dc6011be12974fbf1Two GB10s at TP=2, or three at TP=3 over a ring of direct links: @Bizuayeu served it at both sizes. 160.2 GiB of weights; at TP=2 each GB10 holds 6.6 GiB less than at block 16.Native CUDA, in 1.2.3 (#2041). Refitted from BF16 at block 32 with XSFP4's smoothing, each row's scales packed (, read only by this path), at XSFP4's speed. Its KL and top-1 are nearer BF16 than NVIDIA's two checkpoints', short of XSFP4's (its card).
tensorfold pull kindlingai/glm-5.3-exlr8-k2-k3-k4@f459f5d0272a529403dd9b3fd32f771f4250a0d4 --exlr8 home --node 0/2 --dir ~/models/glm-5.3-exlr8-homeTwo M5 Ultra Macs, 256 GB each; about 160 GB resident per Mac at 8k context / four streams.Two-Mac recipe. Use on the other Mac; Thunderbolt 5 and MCDMA required. No CUDA backend.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B, MLX 4 / 6 / 8-bittensorfold pull LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B-MLX-4bit@667408d494bde191c2cb9dd4f4549827816b9275tensorfold pull LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B-MLX-6bit@1deec53eb49571e21cdcbf82fd5839248f07ed88tensorfold pull LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B-MLX-8bit@67ab417dd02d0c9545802a726df668620eae049dOne Mac (M4 Pro checked), or one NVIDIA GPU with the 4-bit export (GB10 checked).
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MLX with MTPtensorfold pull TensorFold/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-MLX-4bit-MTP@81169a9bc511a27c1b4eedb77a2cd98ced431847One GB10; 20.9 GB checkpoint.Qwen3.6. Native CUDA receipt here. Metal also registers this model type; the recipe's Metal commands describe Python 0.6.6.
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, NVIDIA NVFP4 with MTPtensorfold pull nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4@1355db6a052410cfd62085d94b58866fd0f2c3c5One GB10; 20.3 GiB on the device, 20.9 GiB with the drafter.Native CUDA. Serve with naming the same checkpoint for MTP drafts.
tensorfold pull mlx-community/gemma-4-31B-it-4bit@696d436c404745a59f30e4939a658162b0a9e57ftensorfold pull z-lab/gemma-4-31B-it-DFlash@eabd648301ce28583cc14757912e5e0f84e152e1One Mac (M5 Ultra checked), or one GB10 on CUDA. Pre-M5 Metal has a row path; its assistant and DFlash drafters require M5 tensor units.
Gemma 4 12B, converted MLX 4-bithf download google/gemma-4-12B-it --revision 707f0a3b8a3c7ad586ed01e27eafbad8a27dd0f7 --local-dir ~/models/gemma-4-12b-hfhf download google/gemma-4-12B-it-assistant --revision 46d4c6f13f0ac0ad827b915669b8df9b81c64c51 --local-dir ~/models/gemma-4-12b-assistantOne Mac (M5 Ultra checked); converted text weights 6.3 GB, image weights 100 MB, plus assistant/caches. MLX 4-bit also served on one GB10. Pre-M5 Metal has a row path; the MTP assistant requires M5 tensor units.
Step-5-Preview, converted affinehf download stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview --local-dir ~/models/step5-preview-fp8One 256 GB Mac; text 166.9 GiB, MTP adds 2.5 GiB and vision 3.7 GiB.Convert and serve. The documented 256 GB setup serves converted affine weights; converting the upstream FP8 download needs Python and mlx.
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, community affine 3/4-bithf download BobClawblaw/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix34 --revision 9524999057e0d277d26438606e033e2191fb465c --local-dir ~/models/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix34hf download BobClawblaw/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix256k --revision 916e7ca1044f1c3e7566163096243c940327224d --local-dir ~/models/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash-MLX-mix256kOne 256 GB M5 Ultra; 203.7 GiB (32,768-token window) or 189.2 GiB (147,456), plus caches.MiniMax-M3.1-Flash. Set ; images with . Community checkpoints: lossy conversions of MiniMax's NVFP4 release (KL 0.244 / 0.295). MiniMax Community License.
Kolibri-1, block FP8 (research)tensorfold pull Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1@e52eb4627d11516b0c01de49210ab5a4e4061444One NVIDIA GPU; GB10 measured; 74 GB checkpoint.Kolibri. Text only; copy drafts, no EAGLE-3/neural drafter.
Liquid AI d1-3B, decisionsNative CUDA; RAM minimum not published.
Drama 3 pruned NVFP4, speechhf download plotarmordev/drama-3-NVFP4-Pruned --revision 494db08481db952f834b2241bce63fb3dfa72554 --local-dir drama-3-NVFP4-PrunedNative Metal; roughly 21 GiB checkpoint plus runtime state. Not a minimum-RAM or cross-backend quality claim.Packed experts, BF16 dense/tower weights and FP32 accumulation; no conversion. Use serve drama-3-NVFP4-Pruned --cfg-gamma 1.5 --cfg-batched with an attested catalog voice.

GLM-5.3: one machine or two?

The native release does not qualify GLM-5.3 on one machine. GLM-5.3 EXLR8 needs two 256 GB M5 Ultra Macs; its recipe gives both pull and serve commands. GLM-5.3-Flash is a different model: its native Metal setup needs two M5 Ultras. Native CUDA has recorded TP=2 and TP=3 setups, including FP4-Local and XSFP4 on two and three GB10s. The single-256-GB-Mac GLM-5.3-Flash command in the older recipe is for Python 0.6.6, not this release. For the NVFP4 path, see GLM-5.3-Flash on CUDA and what the contributed run on two GB10s covered.

DeepSeek checkpoints are by any release binary: whole-model gate #827 is still open. MiMo's native backend is not in a release yet. Bonsai's ternary pack and Gemma 4 26B-A4B remain Python-only; they are not native download recommendations. Known issues lists current limits, including Flash Next shared-session cache/performance behavior and the 27B's drafter limits.

Every accepted draft must equal the token the same native engine would produce with . A resumed request must equal fresh execution, and each concurrent stream must equal its solo run. The comparison fixes the checkpoint, backend, settings and runtime. Different quantizations and different backends can produce different outputs. Flash Next on Metal uses shared target rounds with an explicit above one, when that many sessions fit. A lone greedy request there uses GPU-side rounds and hands over when a second request arrives. (the default) and , learning and two-Mac serving use the single-reply driver. restores serial MTP drafting on the shared host. The earlier MTP chain receipt records its own pinned commits. Nemotron, GLM, the 2B model and Qwen3.8-27B use shared lane rounds. On Metal, each of up to 128 streams in the 27B's shared rounds drafts its own DFlash2 tree.

tensorfold pull TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit
tensorfold models
tensorfold models --json
tensorfold info TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit

downloads a checkpoint into the Hugging Face cache and checks what it downloads against the Hub: large files by sha256, small files by their git blob sha1. Large files come down in pieces over up to 16 connections, and an interrupted pull resumes with the pieces it lacks. It refuses a checkpoint whose has no native family, and fetches the 27B's DFlash2 drafter for . lists the cached checkpoints with a model type it knows, and shows one checkpoint's family, format, context and memory floor. prints the same list as one document for programs: 1, and each checkpoint's , and ; is a display title and is the key to match on. serves a cached checkpoint by its repository name.

Compaction is off by default, and with it off every reply is unchanged. With , a conversation that would overflow is compacted instead of refused. The server keeps the system prompt and the most recent turns word for word, and never separates a tool call from its result. The older turns become a memory note: goal, constraints, progress, decisions, next steps, exact names and numbers, and the files the tool calls read or changed. Each later compaction updates the previous note instead of starting over. A client that sends back the compacted conversation keeps its note. The reply carries the note and the compaction counts under , and every reply reports and . The same request gives the same compaction and the same reply. With , the stored note carries over between requests.

Off by default. gives every chat request Cortheon's reasoning program and web research run by the server, so any OpenAI-compatible client gets it with no setup. The model works through Cortheon's stages for its task type and can call and , which the server runs without the client seeing them. A question about current facts, or a request to build with an outside library, is researched before the model starts. A coding task that changed files is asked to run its tests before it finishes. Web text is filtered for instructions aimed at the model, and reads reach public addresses only. With the flag, search queries written from the conversation go to DuckDuckGo, or to Brave with , and pages are fetched from this machine; without it, the server makes no searches and reads no pages. See Cortheon mode.

(also ) advertises each served name and alias. When the engine reports a finite context window, each entry includes equal and integer extensions. These are the loaded engine's effective prompt-plus-reply token limit, including any startup memory fitting; they are not the default reply limit. An unspecified engine window omits both fields. Clients should still handle per-request memory refusals: an advertised context is not a guarantee that every workload fits.

A model that thinks also carries an OpenRouter-style : , (only with ), and , the levels its template names, highest first, then when the template has a thinking switch. A template that names no level leaves out. These describe chat and Responses requests.

The read-only diagnostics report process footprint and lifetime peak, available backend allocation counters, and the applied retained-prefix plan without changing memory policy.

The binary's response lists its supported flags and platform-specific values. prints usage without loading a model.

An existing PATH, or a directory other users can write to (unless sticky, like ), is refused, and connections from other users are closed. API keys, and the Host check apply as on TCP (a client sends a loopback or one in ): the socket's permissions are a second layer, not a substitute for keys.

An external drafter, as a directory or a repo id in the Hugging Face cache, for models that take one: Qwen3.8-27B uses DFlash2 and Gemma 4 31B the drafter named in its recipe. Without one they decode plain.
Drafter weight precision where the model offers a choice: 4 bits (the default), or 0 to keep bf16. Qwen3.8-27B on CUDA takes 4 only.

Metal Drama speech: semantic guidance strength, finite 1–5; 0/default disables it. Only reference-conditioned requests are guided. Enabled replies report ; codec heads stay conditional.
--cfg-allow-request-gammaMetal Drama speech: allow a finite 1–5 request header; invalid values return 400 before engine submission. Without this opt-in, the server's gamma is fixed.

With enabled Metal Drama guidance, submit both independent backbone states in one command buffer rather than separate submissions. Weights are shared; extra state is included in admission. Not vectorized batching.
--silence-floor-dbfs DBFSDrama speech only: explicit frame-power floor for the silence guard, with no default floor. Calibrate below quiet intended speech using public or built-in speech.
--silence-seconds SECONDSDrama speech only: stop after this continuous duration below the explicit floor, retaining audio and reporting . Unset by default: off; calibrate above intentional pauses.

Also keep each conversation's memory note as a Markdown file in DIR.

applies to Nemotron, Flash Next, GLM, Qwen3.8-27B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B, and to the same models but GLM. keeps shared prompt prefixes, such as a system prompt and its tools, on disk, so new conversations resume them after a restart or an upgrade that computes the same bits. It covers GLM-5.3-Flash, Nemotron, and Flash Next on one Mac; Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5-2B, LFM2.5-24B-A2B, GLM-5.3 (EXLR8) and a CUDA server refuse it at startup. Qwen3.8-27B on Metal also resumes a follow-up turn from the state its last reply left in the server's first slot, when the prompt cache holds nothing as far: the turn reads only its new tokens, even on a Mac whose cache cannot keep a long conversation. Where the cache cannot keep a whole context, the server also keeps that slot's DeltaNet states at each prompt's history end, so a turn whose template drops the last reply's reasoning resumes there. Replies are the same tokens as a fresh prompt pass; turns both off.

Sampling defaults come from the checkpoint's , then serve flags and request fields override them. is family-specific; use a positive limit for GLM and inspect the capacity reported at startup. The supported environment variables are listed in , including API keys, request logging and Hugging Face cache paths. makes a native Metal Qwen3.8-27B server log a per-class GPU-time breakdown every N decode rounds ( means 64) and add to its replies; it is diagnostic only, and a profiled round runs slower.

Use the Zig version pinned in , currently 0.17.0. The sources need Xcode's Metal compiler. Install full Xcode and its Metal Toolchain component (xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain); the Command Line Tools alone fail every kernel compile with unable to find utility "metal".

zig build native -Dcpu=apple_m1
zig build test test-golden -Dcpu=apple_m1

Structured output and required tool calls need the release archive's or zig build grammar -Dxgrammar=DIR; prepare DIR with git clone --branch v0.2.8 --recurse-submodules https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar (use the native build's same for grammar).

To build one stripped server for one GPU (zig build -Dgpu=spark -Dnvcc=..., about 69% smaller than the four-target server), see Build a server for one GPU.

On macOS, also runs available Metal device checks. See CONTRIBUTING.md for the host-test subset.

The server is zig-out/native/bin/tensorfold-native. Release archives include the native executable, runtime assets and license notices; packaging describes the qualified CUDA inputs. For cache-aware performance receipts, see observed cache benchmark evidence. The clients retain server usage and output fingerprints, and verify cold/reused states rather than inferring them.

items.title: QwenLM/qwen-code
items.content:
An open-source AI coding agent that lives in your terminal.

  • — Auto-Memory, Auto-Skills, SubAgents, Agent Teams, and MCP. Dynamic workflows, zero setup.
  • Open-source, inside and out — The framework and the Qwen models are open-source. They evolve together. No vendor lock-in.
  • — Supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Qwen APIs. Any third-party provider or local model (Ollama / vLLM). Switch at runtime.
  • — IDE plugins, Desktop app, Web UI, SDKs, and chat integrations (Telegram / DingTalk / WeChat / Feishu).

Qwen Code is actively iterating on itself — using its own agent and models to file issues, submit PRs, review code, and run tests. Powered by the community, driven by AI.

Looking for ? Get started here. The instructions below are for the main version.

curl -fsSL https://qwen-code-assets.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/installation/install-qwen-standalone.sh | bash

irm https://qwen-code-assets.oss-cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/installation/install-qwen-standalone.ps1 | iex

Restart your terminal after installation to ensure environment variables take effect.

Open a terminal in your project and start Qwen Code:

cd /path/to/your-project
qwen

Inside the session, run and choose Qwen Account with Subscription to sign in with your , or configure a provider with an API key. Then try:

Explain this repository and show me where to start.

Choose the interface that fits your workflow:

For automation and custom integrations:

Run Qwen Code as a long-lived service when you want browser, editor, SDK, and automation clients to share agent sessions without each starting a separate process. The daemon provides the built-in Web Shell and an HTTP + SSE API, supports multiple workspaces, and lets clients reconnect to active sessions.

Start it in the foreground and open the Web Shell:

The default address is . To run and manage it in the background instead:

qwen daemon start
qwen daemon status
qwen daemon logs -f
qwen daemon stop

By default, the daemon listens on loopback without bearer authentication; any local process that can reach it can use the full API, including code execution. On shared or untrusted hosts, set and use . See the Daemon guide for workspaces, authentication, remote access, and the API.

SubAgents, Agent Teams, Dynamic Workflows
Auto-Memory, Auto-Skills, Hooks
Built-in Skills (/review, /batch, /loop, /bugfix…)
MCP, Plan Mode, LSP Integration
Auto Mode, Sandbox, Git Worktrees
Computer Use (desktop automation)
IDE Plugins (VS Code / JetBrains / Zed)
Headless Mode, Session Management
Open-source — model and framework
Multi-protocol (OpenAI / Anthropic / Gemini / Qwen + any provider)
Agent Arena (multi-model head-to-head on same task)
Daemon Mode — (multi-client shared agent)
IM Channels (Telegram / DingTalk / WeChat / Feishu)

On , seven Qwen Code versions scored on average using the same Qwen 3.7 Max model (500 tasks, three trials per version).

  • — A modern GUI for command-line AI tools including Qwen Code

  • — Realtime full-duplex voice frontend for Qwen Code over ACP — talk hands-free with barge-in and a local wake word

  • — Let other agents (Claude, Codex, etc.) delegate coding tasks to Qwen Code via ACP. Paste this prompt into your agent:

Use Qwen Code as a coding agent. First, fetch and read this skill reference:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/refs/heads/main/.qwen/skills/qwen-code-claw/SKILL.md
Then follow the instructions inside to install, authenticate, and use Qwen Code via acpx for all coding tasks.
  • — Official CLI for Aliyun's AI platform (). Extends Qwen Code with image/video generation, knowledge retrieval, app orchestration, and model deployment

This project was originally based on Google Gemini CLI v0.8.2. We gratefully acknowledge the Gemini CLI team's excellent work. Starting from Qwen Code v0.1, we stopped syncing with upstream and began independent development as a multi-protocol, multi-platform agent framework with deep integrations for Qwen models and beyond.

items.title: pookjw/HermesEnabler
items.content:
Enable Hermès Watch Faces on any Apple Watch devices

Supported only on watchOS 27.0 through 27.3 beta 1.

On macOS you can install the prebuilt IPA with Sideloadly or build the app directly with Xcode. Either way, the iPhone must be paired with the target Apple Watch, and the Watch must run a supported watchOS version.

Known issue with Sideloadly 0.72:Issue #43 reports that this version may remove the embedded Watch app while signing. If the iPhone app installs but HermesEnabler2 is missing from the Watch, use Xcode instead. This report is specific to version 0.72; compatibility with other versions has not been confirmed.

  1. Install Sideloadly on your Mac, connect your iPhone with a cable, and select it in Sideloadly.
  2. Drag the IPA into Sideloadly and enter your Apple ID. Turn off , set a fixed Bundle Identifier, and start signing.
  3. On the iPhone, open Settings → General → VPN & Device Management and trust your developer certificate.
  4. On the iPhone, open Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode, turn it on, restart, and confirm.
  5. On the iPhone, open the app, go to , and install on the Watch.
  6. On the Apple Watch, open Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode, turn it on, restart, and confirm. If the option is not shown, install the Watch app first and check again.
  7. Open on your Apple Watch and follow the steps in the app.
  1. Select your Apple Watch as the run destination and click .
  2. Open on your Apple Watch and follow the steps in the app.

Windows uses WatchBridge, a community tool that prepares Developer Mode and installs an IPA containing both an iPhone host app and a Watch app. It is not affiliated with Apple or with this project.

  1. Install Apple Mobile Device Service by installing iTunes or the app from the Microsoft Store. WatchBridge needs it for USB and Wi-Fi communication. WebView2 is built into Windows 11.
  2. Make sure your iPhone is paired with the target Apple Watch. WatchBridge supports only one paired Watch at a time; if more than one is paired, the preparation step stops instead of guessing.
  3. Download from WatchBridge Releases, extract it, and run . The executable is unsigned, so Windows SmartScreen may warn on first launch.
  4. Download the IPA from Releases. Use the original IPA that contains both the iPhone host and the ; Watch-only packages are not supported.
  5. Connect the paired iPhone over USB and select it in WatchBridge.
  6. Pair the Watch and confirm the trust prompt on the Watch. Request the switch, then on the Watch open Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Mode, turn it on, restart, and confirm. Return to WatchBridge and click . WatchBridge does not enable Developer Mode or restart the Watch for you.
  7. Sign in with your Apple ID, select the HermesEnabler2 IPA, and start signing and installation. WatchBridge installs the iPhone host app first, then the Watch app.
  8. Open on your Apple Watch and follow the steps in the app.

Developer-mode preparation requires a USB connection. After pairing over USB once, installs and renewals can use Wi-Fi.

  • In Sideloadly, disable and use a fixed Bundle Identifier. Keep the same Bundle Identifier and Apple ID for every update so the app can retain its existing data and backup.
  • Free Apple Personal Team provisioning profiles expire after seven days. When that happens, rebuild and reinstall the app, using the same Apple ID and Bundle Identifier.
  • This project uses an entitlement, which a free Personal Team cannot provision. A paid developer team may be required; changing the Bundle Identifier does not remove this limitation. Do not assume that removing the entitlement is a complete fix, as the app's main functionality without it has not been confirmed.
  • If the iPhone app installs but the Watch app does not appear, check the Sideloadly log for Watch apps will be stripped from the IPA. This means the embedded Watch app was removed; installing the iPhone app alone will not install it. Use Xcode to install the Watch app.
  • Before deleting the app, always restore your MobileGestalt backup through the HermesEnabler2 app.

This project incorporates code from Gester.

items.title: nvm-sh/nvm
items.content:
Node Version Manager - POSIX-compliant bash script to manage multiple active node.js versions.

allows you to quickly install and use different versions of node via the command line.

$ nvm install 24
Now using node v24.14.0 (npm v11.9.0)
$ node -v
v24.14.0
$ nvm use 22
Now using node v22.22.1 (npm v10.9.4)
$ node -v
v22.22.1
$ nvm use 20
Now using node v20.20.1 (npm v10.8.2)
$ node -v
v20.20.1

nvm is a version manager for node.js, designed to be installed per-user, and invoked per-shell. works on any POSIX-compliant shell (sh, dash, ksh, zsh, bash), in particular on these platforms: unix, macOS, and Windows WSL.

To or nvm, you should run the install script. To do that, you may either download and run the script manually, or use the following cURL or Wget command:

curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash

wget -qO- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash

Running either of the above commands downloads a script and runs it. The script clones the nvm repository to , and attempts to add the source lines from the snippet below to the correct profile file (, , , or ). If you find the install script is updating the wrong profile file, set the env var to the profile file’s path, and then rerun the installation script.

export NVM_DIR="$([ -z "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME-}" ] && printf %s "${HOME}/.nvm" || printf %s "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME}/nvm")"
[ -s "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" ] && \. "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" # This loads nvm

  • If the environment variable is present, it will place the files there.

  • You can add to the end of the above script to postpone using until you manually it:

export NVM_DIR="$([ -z "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME-}" ] && printf %s "${HOME}/.nvm" || printf %s "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME}/nvm")"
[ -s "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" ] && \. "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" --no-use # This loads nvm, without auto-using the default version

  • You can customize the install source, directory, profile, and version using the , , , and variables. Eg: curl ... | NVM_DIR="path/to/nvm". Ensure that the does not contain a trailing slash.

  • The installer can use , , or to download , whichever is available.

  • You can instruct the installer to not edit your shell config (for example if you already get completions via a zsh nvm plugin) by setting before running the script. Here's an example one-line command to do that: PROFILE=/dev/null bash -c 'curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash'

When invoking bash as a non-interactive shell, like in a Docker container, none of the regular profile files are sourced. In order to use , , and like normal, you can instead specify the special variable, which bash sources when invoked non-interactively.

# Use bash for the shell
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]

# Create a script file sourced by both interactive and non-interactive bash shells
ENV BASH_ENV="${HOME:-/root}/.bash_env"
RUN touch "${BASH_ENV}"
RUN echo '. "${BASH_ENV}"' >> ~/.bashrc

# Download and install nvm
RUN curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | PROFILE="${BASH_ENV}" bash
RUN echo node > .nvmrc
RUN nvm install
Installing in Docker for CICD-Jobs
FROM ubuntu:latest
ARG NODE_VERSION=20

# install curl
RUN apt update && apt install curl -y

# install nvm
RUN curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash

# set env
ENV NVM_DIR="${HOME:-/root}/.nvm"

# install node
RUN bash -c "source $NVM_DIR/nvm.sh && nvm install $NODE_VERSION"

# set ENTRYPOINT for reloading nvm-environment
ENTRYPOINT ["bash", "-c", "source $NVM_DIR/nvm.sh && exec \"$@\"", "--"]

# set cmd to bash
CMD ["/bin/bash"]

This example defaults to installation of nodejs version 20.x.y. Optionally you can easily override the version with docker build args like:

docker build -t nvmimage --build-arg NODE_VERSION=19 .

After creation of the image you can start container interactively and run commands, for example:

docker run --rm -it nvmimage

root@0a6b5a237c14:/# nvm -v
0.41.0

root@0a6b5a237c14:/# node -v
v19.9.0

root@0a6b5a237c14:/# npm -v
9.6.3

user@host:/tmp/test $ docker run --rm -it nvmimage node -v
v19.9.0
user@host:/tmp/test $ docker run --rm -it nvmimage npm -v
9.6.3

On Linux, after running the install script, if you get or see no feedback from your terminal after you type , simply close your current terminal, open a new terminal, and try verifying again. Alternatively, you can run the following commands for the different shells on the command line:

These should pick up the command.

Since OS X 10.9, has been preset by Xcode command line tools, which means we can't properly detect if Git is installed or not. You need to manually install the Xcode command line tools before running the install script, otherwise, it'll fail. (see #1782)

If you get after running the install script, one of the following might be the reason:

  • Since macOS 10.15, the default shell is and nvm will look for to update, none is installed by default. Create one with and run the install script again.

  • If you use bash, the previous default shell, your system may not have or files where the command is set up. Create one of them with or and run the install script again. Then, run or to pick up the command.

  • You have previously used , but you have installed. You need to manually add these lines to and run .

  • You might need to restart your terminal instance or run . Restarting your terminal/opening a new tab/window, or running the source command will load the command and the new configuration.

  • If the above didn't help, you might need to restart your terminal instance. Try opening a new tab/window in your terminal and retry.

If the above doesn't fix the problem, you may try the following:

  • If you use bash, it may be that your (or ) does not source your properly. You could fix this by adding source ~/<your_profile_file> to it or following the next step below.

  • For more information about this issue and possible workarounds, please refer here

For Macs with the Apple Silicon chip, node started offering arch Darwin packages since v16.0.0 and experimental support when compiling from source since v14.17.0. If you are facing issues installing node using , you may want to update to one of those versions or later.

- name: Install nvm
  ansible.builtin.shell: >
    curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash
  args:
    creates: "{{ ansible_env.HOME }}/.nvm/nvm.sh"

To verify that nvm has been installed, do:

which should output if the installation was successful. Please note that will not work, since is a sourced shell function, not an executable binary.

On Linux, after running the install script, if you get or see no feedback from your terminal after you type , simply close your current terminal, open a new terminal, and try verifying again.

If you're running a system without prepackaged binary available, which means you're going to install node or io.js from its source code, you need to make sure your system has a C++ compiler. For OS X, Xcode will work, for Debian/Ubuntu based GNU/Linux, the and packages work.

also supports Windows in some cases. It should work through WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) depending on the version of WSL. It should also work with Git Bash (MSYS) or Cygwin. Otherwise, for Windows, a few alternatives exist, which are neither supported nor developed by us:

does not support Fish either (see #303). Alternatives exist, which are neither supported nor developed by us:

  • bass allows you to use utilities written for Bash in fish shell
  • fast-nvm-fish only works with version numbers (not aliases) but doesn't significantly slow your shell startup
  • nvm.fish - The Node.js version manager you'll adore, crafted just for Fish
  • fish-nvm - Wrapper around nvm for fish, delays sourcing nvm until it's actually used.

We still have some problems with FreeBSD, because there is no official pre-built binary for FreeBSD, and building from source may need patches; see the issue ticket:

On OS X, if you do not have Xcode installed and you do not wish to download the ~4.3GB file, you can install the . You can check out this blog post on how to just that:

On OS X, if you have/had a "system" node installed and want to install modules globally, keep in mind that:

  • When using you do not need to globally install a module with , so instead of doing sudo npm install -g grunt, do instead
  • If you have an file, make sure it does not contain any settings (which is not compatible with )

Migrating Global Packages While Installing

If you want to install a new version of Node.js and migrate npm packages from a previous version:

nvm install --reinstall-packages-from=node node

This will first use "nvm version node" to identify the current version you're migrating packages from. Then it resolves the new version to install from the remote server and installs it. Lastly, it runs "nvm reinstall-packages" to reinstall the npm packages from your prior version of Node to the new one.

You can also install and migrate npm packages from specific versions of Node like this:

nvm install --reinstall-packages-from=5 6
nvm install --reinstall-packages-from=iojs v4.2

Note that reinstalling packages explicitly does not update the npm version — this is to ensure that npm isn't accidentally upgraded to a broken version for the new node version.

To update npm at the same time add the flag, like this:

nvm install --reinstall-packages-from=default --latest-npm 'lts/*'

Migrating Global Packages Between Installed Versions

--reinstall-packages-from is tied to . To migrate global npm packages between versions you have installed, without (re)installing anything, the destination and run as a standalone command, pointing at the version you want to copy :

nvm use 22.22.2

This reinstalls all global packages from into the currently-active version (). As with --reinstall-packages-from, the npm version itself is not changed.

If you've previously downloaded a node version (or it's still in the cache), you can install it without any network access using the flag:

nvm install --offline 14.7.0

This resolves versions using only locally installed versions and cached downloads. It will not attempt to download anything. This is useful in air-gapped environments, on planes, or when you want to avoid network latency.

A download is only added to the cache () once its checksum has been verified. does not verify cached archives again, so anything placed in the cache by other means is trusted as-is.

You can combine with to install the latest cached LTS version (as long as LTS aliases have been populated by a prior ):

Calling automatically in a directory with a file

In your profile (, , , or ), add the following to whenever you enter a new directory:

Put the following at the end of your :

cdnvm() {
    command cd "$@" || return $?
    nvm_path="$(nvm_find_up .nvmrc | command tr -d '\n')"

    # If there are no .nvmrc file, use the default nvm version
    if [[ ! $nvm_path = *[^[:space:]]* ]]; then

        declare default_version
        default_version="$(nvm version default)"

        # If there is no default version, set it to `node`
        # This will use the latest version on your machine
        if [ $default_version = 'N/A' ]; then
            nvm alias default node
            default_version=$(nvm version default)
        fi

        # If the current version is not the default version, set it to use the default version
        if [ "$(nvm current)" != "${default_version}" ]; then
            nvm use default
        fi
    elif [[ -s "${nvm_path}/.nvmrc" && -r "${nvm_path}/.nvmrc" ]]; then
        declare nvm_version
        # Let nvm parse `.nvmrc`, so that comments are ignored and the content of an invalid
        # or symlinked `.nvmrc` is not passed along to other nvm commands, which may print it
        nvm_version="$(nvm_process_nvmrc "${nvm_path}/.nvmrc")" || return

        declare locally_resolved_nvm_version
        # `nvm ls` will check all locally-available versions
        # If there are multiple matching versions, take the latest one
        # Remove the `->` and `*` characters and spaces
        # `locally_resolved_nvm_version` will be `N/A` if no local versions are found
        locally_resolved_nvm_version=$(nvm ls --no-colors "${nvm_version}" | command tail -1 | command tr -d '\->*' | command tr -d '[:space:]')

        # If it is not already installed, install it
        # `nvm install` will implicitly use the newly-installed version
        if [ "${locally_resolved_nvm_version}" = 'N/A' ]; then
            nvm install "${nvm_version}";
        elif [ "$(nvm current)" != "${locally_resolved_nvm_version}" ]; then
            nvm use "${nvm_version}";
        fi
    fi
}

alias cd='cdnvm'
cdnvm "$PWD" || exit

Installing nvm on Alpine Linux

In order to provide the best performance (and other optimizations), nvm will download and install pre-compiled binaries for Node (and npm) when you run . The Node project compiles, tests and hosts/provides these pre-compiled binaries which are built for mainstream/traditional Linux distributions (such as Debian, Ubuntu, CentOS, RedHat et al).

Alpine Linux, unlike mainstream/traditional Linux distributions, is based on BusyBox, a very compact (~5MB) Linux distribution. BusyBox (and thus Alpine Linux) uses a different C/C++ stack to most mainstream/traditional Linux distributions - musl. This makes binary programs built for such mainstream/traditional distributions incompatible with Alpine Linux, so on and nvm requests a build instead. nodejs.org publishes those only for some recent releases, so for anything else the download 404s and falls back to compiling from source, unless you point it at a mirror that has one (see Platforms without official binaries).

There is a flag for which requests nvm download Node source and compile it locally.

If installing nvm on Alpine Linux still what you want or need to do, you should be able to achieve this by running the following from your Alpine Linux shell, depending on which version you are using:

apk add -U curl bash ca-certificates openssl ncurses coreutils python3 make gcc g++ libgcc linux-headers grep util-linux binutils findutils
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash

apk add -U curl bash ca-certificates openssl ncurses coreutils python2 make gcc g++ libgcc linux-headers grep util-linux binutils findutils
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash

Note: Alpine 3.5 can only install NodeJS versions up to v6.9.5, Alpine 3.6 can only install versions up to v6.10.3, Alpine 3.7 installs versions up to v8.9.3, Alpine 3.8 installs versions up to v8.14.0, Alpine 3.9 installs versions up to v10.19.0, Alpine 3.10 installs versions up to v10.24.1, Alpine 3.11 installs versions up to v12.22.6, Alpine 3.12 installs versions up to v12.22.12, Alpine 3.13 & 3.14 install versions up to v14.20.0, Alpine 3.15 & 3.16 install versions up to v16.16.0 (These are all versions on the main branch). Alpine 3.5 - 3.12 required the package to build NodeJS, as they are older versions to build. Alpine 3.13+ requires to successfully build newer NodeJS versions, but you can use with Alpine 3.13+ if you need to build versions of node supported in Alpine 3.5 - 3.15, you just need to specify what version of NodeJS you need to install in the package install script.

The Node project now publishes an official binary for some recent releases (v24.20.0+ and v26.8.0+; no v25 release has one). There is no official musl binary.

To make development and testing work easier we supply a Dockerfile for development usage. It's based on an Ubuntu base image prepared with essential and useful tools for development. To build the docker image of the environment, do a Docker build at the root of repository:

$ docker build -t nvm-dev .

This will package your current nvm working copy with our pre-defined development environment into a Docker image named . After the build you should see it appear in the list of images:

$ docker images

REPOSITORY         TAG                 IMAGE ID            CREATED             SIZE
nvm-dev            latest              9ca4c57a97d8        7 days ago          650 MB

To start and enter a container based on this image:

$ docker run -h nvm-dev -it nvm-dev

nvm@nvm-dev:~/.nvm$

It takes several minutes to build the image and the image size is about 650MB, so it's not suitable for production usage.

  • If you try to install a node version and the installation fails, be sure to run to delete cached node downloads, or you might get an error like the following:

    curl: (33) HTTP server doesn't seem to support byte ranges. Cannot resume.

  • Where's my ? Check out #43

  • After the v0.8.6 release of node, nvm tries to install from binary packages. But in some systems, the official binary packages don't work due to incompatibility of shared libs. In such cases, use option to force install from source:

  • If setting the alias does not establish the node version in new shells (i.e. yields ), ensure that the system's node is set before the source line in your shell profile (see #658)

nvm node version not found in vim shell

If you set node version to a version other than your system node version and open vim and run you should see if you see your system version . You need to run:

sudo chmod ugo-x /usr/libexec/path_helper

nvm is not compatible with the npm config "prefix" option

Some solutions for this issue can be found here

There is one more edge case causing this issue, and that's a mismatch between the path and the user's home directory's actual name.

You have to make sure that the user directory name in and the user directory name you'd see from running are capitalized the same way (See this issue).

To change the user directory and/or account name follow the instructions here

Homebrew makes zsh directories insecure

zsh compinit: insecure directories, run compaudit for list.
Ignore insecure directories and continue [y] or abort compinit [n]? y

Homebrew causes insecure directories like /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions and . This is an problem - it is a homebrew problem. Refer here for some solutions related to the issue.

Macs with Apple Silicon chips

Experimental support for the Apple Silicon chip architecture was added in node.js v15.3 and full support was added in v16.0. Because of this, if you try to install older versions of node as usual, you will probably experience either compilation errors when installing node or out-of-memory errors while running your code.

So, if you want to run a version prior to v16.0 on an Apple Silicon Mac, it may be best to compile node targeting the Intel architecture so that Rosetta 2 can translate the processor instructions to ARM-based Apple Silicon instructions. Here's what you will need to do:

  • Install Rosetta, if you haven't already done so

    $ softwareupdate --install-rosetta

    You might wonder, "how will my Apple Silicon Mac know to use Rosetta for a version of node compiled for an Intel chip?". If an executable contains only Intel instructions, macOS will automatically use Rosetta to translate the instructions.

  • Open a shell that's running using Rosetta

    Note: This same thing can also be accomplished by finding the Terminal or iTerm App in Finder, right clicking, selecting "Get Info", and then checking the box labeled "Open using Rosetta".

    Note: This terminal session is now running in . If is not the shell you typically use, may not be 'd automatically like it probably is for your usual shell through your dotfiles. If that's the case, make sure to source .

    $ source "${NVM_DIR}/nvm.sh"

  • Install whatever older version of node you are interested in. Let's use 12.22.1 as an example. This will fetch the node source code and compile it, which will take several minutes.

    $ nvm install v12.22.1 --shared-zlib

    Note: You're probably curious why is included. There's a bug in recent versions of Apple's system compiler. If one of these broken versions is installed on your system, the above step will likely still succeed even if you didn't include the flag. However, later, when you attempt to something using your old version of node.js, you will see errors. If you want to avoid the possible hassle of dealing with this, include that flag. For more details, see this issue and this comment

  • Exit back to your native shell.

    Note: If you selected the box labeled "Open using Rosetta" rather than running the CLI command in the second step, you will see here. Unless you have another reason to have that box selected, you can deselect it now.

  • Check to make sure the architecture is correct. is the abbreviation for , which is what you want to see.

    $ node -p process.arch
x64

Now you should be able to use node as usual.

If you've encountered this error on WSL-2:

curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.41.0/install.sh | bash
% Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                Dload  Upload  Total   Spent    Left  Speed
0     0    0     0    0     0      0      0 --:--:--  0:00:09 --:--:--     0curl: (6) Could not resolve host: raw.githubusercontent.com

It may be due to your antivirus, VPN, or other reasons.

Where you can while you can't

This could simply be solved by running this in your root directory:

sudo rm /etc/resolv.conf
sudo bash -c 'echo "nameserver 8.8.8.8" > /etc/resolv.conf'
sudo bash -c 'echo "[network]" > /etc/wsl.conf'
sudo bash -c 'echo "generateResolvConf = false" >> /etc/wsl.conf'
sudo chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf

This deletes your file that is automatically generated when you run WSL, creates a new file and puts , then creates a file and adds and generateResolveConf = false to prevent auto-generation of that file.

You can check the contents of the file by running:

Currently, the sole maintainer is @ljharb - more maintainers are quite welcome, and we hope to add folks to the team over time. Governance will be re-evaluated as the project evolves.

Only the latest version (v0.41.0 at this time) is supported.

If you are unable to update to the latest version of , our partners provide commercial security fixes for all unsupported versions:
