Can I query sessions and config over the web? Yes — open http://localhost:8787: an overview dashboard, session list with per-session detail, live logs, a config editor, and an upstream connectivity test. A Blog view renders notes and long-form articles inside the panel itself — bundled with the install, refreshed from GitHub master on a ~1-hour throttle while online (fail-soft to the bundled copy when offline); the full library also lives on GitHub Pages. Everything else is also plain JSON for scripting (, , , …).

When does compression happen? It is model-driven: the injected context tools are called by the model as context grows, gentle growth nudges (~50K-token steps by design, adjustable via compress.nudgeGrowthTokens) prompt it along the way, and preflight fires as a hard backstop when the input alone exceeds the window (#470). Watch it live with or the web UI.

Does compression shrink my client's own conversation file? No — the most common surprise in very long sessions (#5796). Compression shrinks what is sent to the model: every outgoing request is rebuilt from live blocks plus summaries, so the wire stays small however long the conversation runs. The client's stored history is user data — bili never rewrites it. On dsh the host's auto-compaction is additionally disabled while bili is active (two compressors must not fight over one history, #1772/#2474/#3354), so the host-side file grows with every turn: each turn takes longer as it grows (measured: tens of seconds per turn at ~30K messages, #5796), and the practical convergence path is to when it gets heavy. The web session list badges sessions at 5,000+ requests (长会话/slow) as a reminder that this point has been reached.

Why does the first compaction wait until ~200k? Compaction does not trigger on absolute window position but on growth intervals: by default the first soft compaction fires 50k tokens past the boot content (compress.nudgeGrowthTokens, flat and window-independent). With a boot around 100k — or with the growth step set to ~100k — the first compaction may wait until ~200k. To make it fire earlier: 1) trim the system prompt, disable unneeded tools, prune skills; 2) lower compress.nudgeGrowthTokens to ~50k; 3) enable lean mode. Worked example in docs/configuration.md.

Is bili transparent? How do I turn it off? Unrecognized endpoints forward unchanged (docs/clients.md), and every mode reverses cleanly: bili plugin remove <client> for native installs, stop using the launcher command / env vars / prefix for the other two — traffic goes direct again immediately.

Can I combine bili with a model-routing gateway (e.g. magpie)? Yes — point the client at bili, and point bili at the gateway through the prefix, which embeds the gateway's absolute URL: http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425…. Example: Claude Code → ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425 + ; OpenAI-style clients → OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1 (+ ). Compression happens routing — every request that reaches any account in the gateway's routing groups is already compressed. Credentials stay in the gateway: the client's dummy key rides through untouched, and real keys never touch bili. Caveats: ① an account switch mid-conversation invalidates the provider's prefix cache — inherent to multi-account routing, not bili (watch it in the section of ); ② routed model names are opaque to bili's window lookup — declare their context windows under the providers key via , or they run on the fallback window (route-miss warning, #2317); ③ if the relay rejects bili's Anthropic-lane stamps, set ; ④ loopback gateways work out of the box; a gateway on a private non-loopback address may additionally need network.allowPrivateHttpProviders (#2984); ⑤ for Claude Code native plugin mode (bili plugin install claude), set BILI_CLAUDE_UPSTREAM=http://127.0.0.1:3425 before install so the managed block wraps the relay into (or configure ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:3425 directly; and both accepted, #5369). Verified end-to-end over all three wires (OpenAI Chat / Responses / Anthropic Messages, including cross-protocol conversion), #4433.

Does this work with opencodex () — the local Codex/Claude Code gateway with a ChatGPT account pool? Same pattern: point the client at bili, and point bili at ocx through the prefix — OpenAI-style clients (chat completions and Responses, e.g. Codex) → OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:10100/v1; Anthropic-style clients → ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8787/bili/http://127.0.0.1:10100. A dummy key value satisfies clients that require one; it rides through untouched. Keep bili ocx rather than behind it: ocx owns the provider credentials and the account pool at its final hop, so only this order keeps compression and pooling working together. Loopback needs no key between the two (ocx's default loopback bind reads no token); a non-loopback bind takes plus the header per its docs. Request models by ocx's id so routing is deterministic; as with any gateway, routed ids are opaque to bili's window lookup (declare them via ) and a mid-session account rebind invalidates the prefix cache (watch in ). Verified end-to-end over all three wires (OpenAI Chat / Responses / Anthropic Messages), bili 0.1.212 × ocx 2.97.0.

Where are logs and session data stored? Log: ~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log (also mirrored to stderr); session state: ~/.local/share/billion-context/ (XDG-overridable; Windows AV exclusion #362, opt-in cleanup #1082) — full paths in docs/configuration.md.

A ships at the repository root — it installs the published npm package at build time (the tested artifact; nothing is compiled in the image) and runs the proxy as a service:

docker build -t billion-context .
docker run -d --name bili -p 8787:8787 \
  -v bili-config:/root/.config/billion-context \
  -v bili-data:/root/.local/share/billion-context \
  -v bili-cache:/root/.cache/billion-context \
  -v bili-state:/root/.local/state/billion-context \
  billion-context

Then point clients' baseURL at http://<host>:8787/bili/… exactly like Option 3 above.

  • — uses the builtin storage engine directly (no native-addon download). Don't switch to Node 20 bases: the self-downloaded SQLite engine requires Node ≥ 22 and crashes under 20 (#3341).
  • in-container self-update is () — the sanctioned update channel for a containerized copy is rebuilding/pulling a newer image; an in-place self-update would be silently reverted to the image version on the next recreate. Opt back in with ; pin a release at build time with --build-arg BILI_VERSION=0.1.197 (default ).
  • the four mounted dirs hold config, session state, update throttle/lock + cached SQLite engine, and logs respectively. Mount volumes or bind mounts so they survive container replacement; the image also declares them as s so even a bare keeps them out of the container layer.
  • the container listens on so clients outside it can connect — there is , so expose the port only on a trusted network (same caveat as below). The web UI and JSON endpoints work unchanged through the mapped port.
  • the image ships a probing on 8787 via node's builtin fetch (no curl needed in the slim base); if you override the listen port, remember the probe stays pinned to 8787.
bili --port 9000              # change listen port
bili --host 0.0.0.0           # listen on all interfaces (see host note below)
bili --debug                 # verbose logging (also: set "debug": true in config)
bili --passthrough           # forward without compression (smoke-test mode)
bili --config ~/my-bili.json # use a different config file
bili update                  # check & install a newer version now (bypasses throttle)
bili doctor --fix            # converge drifted dsh profile ledgers (manifest spec / lockfile record / bundle copy) to the on-disk version (#3496)
bili --no-auto-update        # disable self-update for this run
bili --auto-restart-on-update   # self-restart when a new version is installed (default off)
bili --bin /path/to/client   # launcher: spawn this exact client binary instead of auto-detecting (env BILI_CLIENT_BIN)

Flags override env vars and the config file. lists them all.

By default the proxy binds and only accepts loopback connections. To serve agents on other machines: (or your LAN IP); remote agents point their model at http://<this-host>:<port>/bili/….

  • MITM-mode then also accepts remote clients — for whitelisted model hosts only. Blind tunnels to arbitrary hosts stay loopback-only, so the proxy can never be used as an open relay.
  • destination admission (#409): the proxy itself and link-local/metadata addresses are always denied; loopback/private destinations are allowed for local clients (self-hosted upstreams) and denied for remote clients unless listed in BILI_TUNNEL_ALLOWED_HOSTS ( or , comma-separated). One exception (#1073): a client relaying a management path (, ) to a destination is forwarded unmarked; remote peers and hostname destinations keep the internal tunnel marker unconditionally, and management paths stay unreachable through the tunnel even via NAT hairpin. An absolute-form request addressed to the instance's own endpoint on a management path is served locally instead of tunneled (a forward-proxy-style health probe gets a real answer).
  • There is : only do this on a trusted LAN or behind a firewall. The management endpoints remain loopback-only. A startup warning reminds you of the above.

(or env , or in config — flag > env > config) logs every (tag counts, token usage), the nudge decision (growth/usage/pendingT1/shouldInject), client headers, and SSE rewrites.

All logs tee to ~/.local/state/billion-context/bili.log by default (XDG state dir) and still print to stderr. Override with in config or ( disables the file). Auto-rotates at 10 MB (). Per-request cache-hit stats log as [acp-usage] round N input=X cached=Y (cache hit Z%) so you can measure prefix-cache health directly from the log.

Connection lifecycle tuning (#1982)

Client-facing connections close gracefully after the final response: when the proxy initiates the close (), it waits up to BILI_POST_RESPONSE_LINGER_MS (default ) for the client's close signal before releasing the socket, so pooled clients see a clean EOF instead of a possible RST from racing bytes. Related knobs: BILI_KEEP_ALIVE_TIMEOUT_MS (idle-reap budget, default ) and BILI_CLIENT_ERROR_BACKSTOP_MS (terminal backstop for the error-drain path, default ) — full semantics in docs/configuration.md.

The proxy checks npm on startup and every 3 minutes; a newer version is installed in place and a notice is logged — , unless you enable opt-in self-restart ( flag, env ACP_AUTO_RESTART_ON_UPDATE=1, or "autoRestartOnUpdate": true in config — default OFF): with zero in-flight requests it verifies the new install, stops accepting connections, drains, spawns a replacement on the same port, and exits once it accepts connections (clients reconnect automatically; session state survives on disk). Safety gates: zero in-flight through the drain window, an install sanity check before re-exec, and a 10-minute cooldown marker so a flapping version can never loop-restart; any failure resumes the original listener and falls back to the plain reminder.

Staggered rollout (#3619): a discovered version is not applied immediately by automatic updates. Each instance draws ONE random moment inside a delay window (built-in default ) and upgrades when it arrives; the drawn moment is persisted, so restarts never re-roll. Fleet upgrades therefore spread across the window instead of completing within minutes of a release, leaving time to catch a bad release mid-rollout (#3401/#3600/#3394). The window plus emergency controls live in a public policy file ( in this repo, fetched anonymously with ETag caching): freezes automatic upgrades fleet-wide, skips listed versions, sets an upgrade ceiling. Fail-open by design — an unreachable or malformed file simply falls back to local defaults, and the file can steer timing/skip/pin only, never what gets installed. Per-machine exits: manual bypasses /stagger (still respects /), + (or BILI_UPDATE_STAGGER_MIN_MS/BILI_UPDATE_STAGGER_MAX_MS) restore legacy immediate upgrades, and disables auto-updates entirely. Full format and semantics: docs/configuration.md → .

While the running process is behind the on-disk install ("stale"), the web UI shows a banner (running vs installed version, auto-restart state) and returns {version, diskVersion, stale, autoRestartOnUpdate, advisory, updatePolicy, inFlight} for scripting ( is the active critical-defect entry or , see below; reports the #3619 rollout state — policy source, //, and the pending staggered upgrade with its due time). Disable permanently via in config or .

In ( / / — the proxy runs embedded in a long-lived host), "restart bili" means restarting the : the embedded process cannot exit on its own, so a host left open keeps serving whatever code it started with, silently missing every fix auto-update reports as installed (#1603). Enable to have it self-restart at a safe point, or run (OpenCode hosts today — pi/dsh coverage tracked in #2084) — the status panel appends a one-line staleness warning (running vs installed version) whenever the on-disk install is ahead of the live process. Auto-update only ever replaces disk files and (optionally) the proxy process; injected code inside the host process only takes effect after the host itself restarts — so if the injection breaks at runtime mid-session (a disposed agent scope, a disabled plugin), model traffic goes direct and uncompressed until then. Since #3581 this state is visible instead of silent: the web UI shows a "takeover broken" banner (agent + refusal count) whenever a plugin reports its attribution gate degraded while no session is live, and / expose the per-agent state (//, refusal count, first-refusal timestamp). Background lanes that are agentless (e.g. dsh's title-generation sidecar) never carry an initiator, so their small one-shot calls go direct by definition; under the #3651 contract these normal interceptions are NEVER reported and therefore can never raise the banner. The banner fires only when the attribution lookup itself throws (an internal host error, e.g. a disposed agent scope), and then names what failed: the thrown error text, the masked endpoint, when the episode started, how many requests went uncompressed, the remedy (restart the host process), plus copy/submit-diagnostics buttons that prefill a GitHub issue.

Update visibility is silent by default since v0.1.183 (#1977): routine/recommended releases no longer render an update line on the panel footer or in — only a -tier release surfaces there (CRITICAL UPDATE READY/AVAILABLE). The standing ways to check an installed-but-not-restarted release are the stale cues above: web UI banner, the one-line warning, and . Deliberately no always-on nag; the advisory channel (#1481) remains the only auto-visible critical path.

When an install keeps failing (unwritable or host-managed dir, network error, …), auto-update no longer re-downloads and retries on every 3-minute cycle forever. After three consecutive failures it backs off exponentially (5 min → 10 → 20 …, capped at 6 h), logs a one-time actionable hint (fix permissions / npm prefix, reinstall user-level, or disable via / ), and logs nothing further about the failure while cooling down (no download, no retry line); it resumes as soon as the failure clears or a different version is targeted (#1603).

The same bounded retry now covers the the global self-update drives instead of writing the copy itself — the dsh desktop in-place copy, the dsh profile bundles, and pi's npm copy (#2192). Each lane keeps its own failure streak keyed by lane + target version, so a persistently broken desktop layout no longer re-downloads the full tarball every cycle (up to ~480 downloads/day per affected machine before the fix); three strikes arms the same exponential cooldown, and the one-time hint names the failing lane and its manual fix (dsh plugin --profile <name> add …, , or recreate the desktop profile). Host-managed instances additionally check on their own slower cadence — 30 minutes plus up to 15 minutes of jitter, tracked under a separate throttle marker — instead of consuming the global 3-minute budget. Failure streaks are shared across every bili process on the machine through a small state file in the cache dir (), so several running instances don't each burn their own retry budget; a clean disarms the dsh profile lane immediately. The file is written atomically (tmp+rename) and every writer merges with what is already on disk, so concurrent instances cooperate instead of overwriting each other's streaks; long-lived processes re-read it when it changes, so a manual disarm by one copy is visible to the others on their next check. It is fail-safe in the retry direction — a corrupt file or jumped clock is dropped, never allowed to silence a lane for long. clears the dsh-profile lane's key; a repaired desktop lane clears its own key on its next successful in-place refresh.

Stale local DNS after a network/VPN change (#5224)

A standalone proxy can keep holding stale OS-resolver state after a WSL/VPN/TUN topology change — the process caches its system resolver and libuv's does not re-read on its own. Symptom: every model request through the tunnel answers HTTP 502 tunnel_destination_denied with detail , even though a freshly started resolves the same host fine at that moment and from a new shell works. Either remedy clears it:

  • Restart the proxy process — a fresh process re-reads the system resolver. In the launcher lanes and the dsh web-profile lane the proxy is a process (the instance registry), so restarting only the client/host re-adopts the same wedged proxy and does help — you must stop and relaunch the proxy itself. (In embedded plugin mode the proxy runs inside the host, so restarting the host clear it.)
  • Route egress through an upstream proxy — or BILI_UPSTREAM_PROXY=… BILI_UPSTREAM_PROXY_MODE=auto: the destination is then resolved remotely by that proxy, so bili never consults its own (stale) resolver for admission.

Critical-defect advisories (forced updates)

Independent of auto-update (#1481): even with off, the proxy polls a small companion npm package (billion-context-advisories, published by CI from this repo's directory) on the same 3-minute cadence. Each advisory names a semver range of broken versions (), the exact version to install ( — which may be than the current one, i.e. a rollback), and a user-facing . When the local version falls inside , bili force-installs through the self-updater's full safety chain (cross-process lock, backup + verify + rollback; source checkouts and host-managed installs are refused with manual instructions instead) and warns prominently: a one-time log line per process per advisory id, a banner on the web UI showing the reason and the exact manual upgrade command, and the active entry under in . The check is fail-open by design: an unreachable or malformed advisory source only produces a warning — model traffic is never blocked by it. Disable via config () or env (); point at a custom document with / .

(#5548) — distinct from the defect advisory above, three sources feed the web-UI banners, and equal ids shadow in the order local file > remote feed > built-in: (1) one-time notices rendered from the UI i18n strings; (2) — drop JSON files into <config dir>/announcements/*.json (~/.config/billion-context/announcements/ by default) and they render automatically: bilingual records with kind-derived color, npm-style targeting (, , , , lists), grey rollout, time windows, and per-kind priority — one bad file disables only itself; (3) — this repo's master branch announcements/remote.json (CI-linted on every PR), fetched on the ~3-minute watcher cadence, whose last-known-good snapshot survives restarts and outages while malformed pushes are rejected; unreachable installs (firewalls) point / at a relay mirror of the same document. Dismissal follows each record's declared mode: (default, content-addressed — editing a notice shows it again), (this process run only), or (renders without a close button). Dismissing a built-in intro notice is recorded per install in bili's unified storage (SQLite by default; the MySQL backend works too), so it survives restarts — the old state file remains only as fallback on legacy-only installs without a unified sidecar. The official feed currently ships an empty entry list.

The full configuration reference — config file location, top-level keys, providers, compression tuning, environment variables — lives in .

One JSON document at ~/.config/billion-context/billion-context.json ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/billion-context/; override the path with ). Precedence when several sources set the same knob: CLI flag (where one exists) > env var > config file > built-in default — every env var keeps working as the override tier.

What's inside (details in docs/configuration.md):

  • — per-provider routing table: upstream override, model context windows, per-provider/model compress tuning, wire-protocol declaration, compaction opt-in.
  • — three-level compression tuning (global → provider → model): thresholds, nudge cadence, preservation rules, prompts, tiers.
  • Server-level blocks — process-wide behavior, including the #2030 additions: (timeouts / retry / keep-alive / preflight cadence), (session persistence format + tail), (cap + GC policy), (registry mirror + check interval), (dumps, render-tag mode, injection switches), , plus scalars / / and extensions , , .
{
  "network": { "upstreamTimeoutMs": 900000 },
  "persist": { "zstd": true },
  "sessions": { "gc": { "enabled": true, "maxAgeDays": 14 } }
}

Knobs people look for first:

  • Upstream proxy (firewall/GFW) — routing the proxy's own outbound traffic through v2rayA/clash: full resolution order, empty-string = explicit direct, SOCKS5 rejection, both egress paths, and the vs key schemes live in docs/configuration.md (Server Settings → ; Providers → key schemes).
  • Wire-compat role rewrite () — an upstream that rejects the role? Covered by docs/configuration.md (Server Settings → ) — including the learn-on-failure auto-fix that needs no configuration at all.
  • Signed upstreams (body-covering signatures) — a gateway whose requests carry a body-covering signature (CodeArts APIG's , or gateway-invented headers like ): the built-in scheme re-signs transparently on dsh; every other detected scheme is ALWAYS refused locally — signed requests are either re-signed+compressed or refused, never passed through unsigned — and bili keeps reminding at startup and in the web UI until it ships the scheme's re-signer (#1884/#2090). Detection rules, per-scheme overrides, and / / live in docs/configuration.md (Server Settings → ).

Using or the native pi plugin () includes built-in subagent support, enabled by default: , , and . This additional tool surface is specific to pi.

Keep only one subagent implementation enabled. If you use the built-in support, remove or disable other pi subagent plugins (for example, or a separately installed billion-context-pi-subagents) in both user and project settings to avoid overlapping tools, prompts, or behavior. If you prefer another subagent plugin, disable the built-in support instead. A install at either scope (project or user) makes the built-in delegate stand down automatically by default — a user-scope install loads in every project, so the guard applies there too (#5637); set to keep alongside it.

To disable the built-in subagents while keeping context compression, merge this into ~/.config/billion-context/billion-context.json (or the file selected by ), preserving your other settings:

{
  "pi": {
    "subagents": false
  }
}

Restart pi and start a new session for the change to take effect. This disables the three delegate tools, their system-prompt section, and the fleet keyboard shortcut; context compression remains enabled. It does not disable independently installed subagent plugins. More options: subagent configuration.

The proxy keys compression state on the conversation value the client itself provides, verbatim () — no hashing, no protocol/upstream/API-key dimensions (those mutate mid-conversation and orphaned state exactly when users kept talking, #280/#286). The id stays inside the proxy (state store, persistence, UI label); it is never sent upstream.

Where the value comes from, first hit wins: the plugin's x-bili-plugin-conversation (honored only alongside the marker header), then per-client headers (, /, , ), then generic headers (, , , , /), then body fields: / on the Responses wire, and promoted over the content-fingerprint fallback on the Responses/OpenAI/Anthropic wires.

/ turn-metadata thread id
header (, the request's own session id; 2.x sends the cache-routing affinity in // alongside it, #2779 — 1.x sent its own id in those instead)
header
promoted over any fingerprint (#268)
nothing → anonymous prefix affinity below

omp caveat (#2583/#3556): on recent OMP builds, default Anthropic () requests leave the host through OMP's Cowork transport over node:https directly — they never reach bili's fetch layer, so the stamp is there (stamping would leak the field into Anthropic's strict schema → HTTP 400). Since #3556 the launcher lane no longer leaves that hole open by default: unless you set / yourself, the launcher exports PI_PROXY_ANTHROPIC=<proxy>, which pushes Cowork onto Bun's fetch and routes it through the proxy like every other lane (compressed and session-visible; the stamped key is consumed and stripped by the proxy). Direct-and-anonymous remains only for native omp mode and for launcher lanes where you pin your own proxy posture; all other omp traffic keeps its stamped identity. Details: docs/technical-notes.md.

omp advisor isolation (#5567): omp's persistent background streams (e.g. a turn-reviewer on a second model) are separate model conversations, but their Chat Completions requests carry no conversation signal of their own — the plugin stamps the main session's id into , so both streams land in ONE bili session. Two models/protocols interleaving into one ledger corrupts it: refs go DEAD ( / ), fold coverage drifts, and usage/window/nudge metering cross-talks between the streams (the log line foreign payload under a shared session id (#4805) marks where the proxy noticed). Until the host-side identity fix lands (tracked in #5567), isolate the advisor by letting it carry its own identity on the wire: in omp's model-registry config (the section of ), set compat.supportsPromptCacheKey: true on the advisor's provider entry — pi-ai then serializes the advisor's own session UUID as , and bili binds it to its own session. Boundaries: this does not help if omp explicitly passes a shared cache key for the advisor; once isolated, the advisor runs as its own session with its own compression state; verify via the web panel that advisor traffic appears under a separate session id.

Header-less clients (pi-like): anonymous prefix affinity. With no conversation signal at all, the proxy resolves the session from the replayed history itself (, #309): a request reattaches to a stored session only when its history reproduces that session's message chain byte-exactly from position 0; otherwise it gets its own deterministic session. Consequences (#1262): a conversation reattaches to its own session (even after a proxy restart, #499); a new task with an identical opener does NOT inherit another conversation's blocks — it mints a fresh, fully separate session; a request with no usable signal at all gets an explicit 400 instead of silently colliding.

For upstream sticky-routing, the proxy forwards only identity values the client already supplied (e.g. a body is forwarded upstream as ); it never synthesizes one itself.

explicit-id clients are safe to run concurrently. For header-less multi-agent use, prefer the client plugin (stamps a stable id per conversation) or pass an explicit header — otherwise prefix affinity still keeps distinct tasks apart (a diverged fork costs one raw resend plus a compression-ladder restart).

Derived (child) sessions inherit the parent's compressed context (#1333, #1362)

A child session (subagent/fork starting from an empty history) reports its lineage at birth — its identity registration carries and the proxy records a read-only link — so / fall back along the parent chain for content the child never saw itself (cycle-guarded, depth cap 8). Nothing is copied into the child, the parent is never modified; if the parent is unknown the child simply starts fresh. Per-lane parent signals (pi/omp header, OpenCode V1/V2 ): docs/session-identity.md. claude/codex/dsh need nothing here: they share one session id across subagents or have no child-session concept at all.

Running multiple instances (#3633)

One conversation belongs to one instance for its whole life. Fold state, prefix affinity and the summary budget are keyed to a session id whose home is the client's own history — and the session's rows live in that instance's . There is no shared store between instances: nothing replicates, nothing fails over, nothing rehydrates a session onto a different instance.

Consequences for anyone tempted to put several instances behind one Service:

  • Sticky routing is required, and affinity is the wrong kind. The conversation identity lives in a header or the request body, not the source IP — a Service can only hash on IP, so a client pinned to replica N silently loses session when replica N dies (buying throughput while selling away availability, exactly when you scaled out because of load). Correct routing is an L7 proxy hashing a conversation header (x-bili-plugin-conversation, , , …) onto a backend — and the client actually sending one (header-less clients get prefix affinity instead, which an L7 proxy cannot hash).
  • Instance count is volume count. The state directory is one local directory with SQLite in WAL mode (); a coherent shared and working byte-range locks across writers require an RWO volume that is never shared. Pointing two instances at the same RWX/NFS path does not give you a shared store — it gives you silent corruption behind a timeout. One RWO volume per instance, included: "unified" means one store (sessions + CCR + CAS in one ), not one store for the fleet.
  • The workload that actually scales is many independent short-lived conversations — one proxy per client or per lane — not one long conversation load-balanced across proxies. Long conversations are single-instance by design.

Single machine, multiple installs (#5046). The topology above covers deployment replicas; one desktop has a sibling situation: two installs on ONE machine (e.g. two DSH profiles — desktop + bot, or a global npm copy beside a host-tree copy) each start their own proxy and, unless isolated, both resolve the SAME default XDG sessions directory and the same config file. Multiple processes writing ONE local-disk is the SUPPORTED topology (#5082/#5091) — SQLite WAL is multi-process safe on a local filesystem — so startup NEVER blocks on a live foreign writer: the peer shows up as an info-level [storage] process pid … is also using … line plus the status wire, nothing more (policy settled 2026-10-31, withdrawing the #5046/B-era refuse-to-start for exactly this shape). What genuinely remains hazardous is two installs walking the SAME concurrently — that case alarms separately (split-brain contest, #3923). If you still want strictly separate histories and stores per install, give each its own (plus when the config should differ too) through that install's launcher/profile environment — no global env changes needed. Once isolated, the notice drops off entirely. Note the distinction from the deployment case above: local disk with SQLite WAL tolerates many writers; shared RWX/NFS storage does NOT and keeps requiring one writer per volume.

Naming note: creates a session (from stored checkpoints), not a pod replica — read it as .

The proxy rewrites each session's state file every turn of a long session; on Windows, real-time AV (Defender), the search indexer, or a sync tool (OneDrive) can lock the sessions dir mid-write, so persists fail with until the lock clears. Fix at the root: add %USERPROFILE%\.local\share\billion-context\ to your antivirus exclusions (Defender steps included) and keep sync tools off that path — docs/configuration.md. The same exclusion also covers the unified-storage refusing to open (unable to open database file, #3823) — the storage-degrade warning names it as the first suspect.

Session file cleanup (#1082)

Short-lived sessions leave small state files behind that are never resumed. Cleanup is (; off by default — session files are user data, no silent deletion policy): when enabled, bili sweeps the sessions dir at boot and hourly and deletes a file only when BOTH hold — older than BILI_SESSION_GC_MAX_AGE_DAYS (default 7 days) AND never compressed with its newest request body ≤ BILI_SESSION_GC_MAX_TOKENS tokens (default 1M) — so deletion loses nothing but bytes. CCR content stores follow their session file's lifecycle; compressed sessions are never deleted; every deletion is audit-logged. Full policy: docs/configuration.md.

Storage maintenance CLI (#3928)

The same store maintenance the panel exposes over HTTP (, POST /__bili/storage/restore) has a thin CLI layer — no proxy needed, run it on any machine that owns the sessions dir:

bili sessions ls                 # id, label, decoded size, last-updated, storage status (active/archived)
bili sessions rm <id>            # full delete (content refcount release incl. media); shrinks index.db afterwards (--no-vacuum skips)
bili sessions archive <id>       # export to archive/archive.jsonl + sweep rows; tombstone keeps label & identity
bili sessions restore <id>       # bring an archived session back from the log line
bili sessions foreign-blocks     # (#5312) list fold blocks whose covered messages never belonged to this transcript — dry-run; --apply reversibly archives them, --restore <sid>:<bid> brings one back
bili storage gc [--days N] [--vacuum full|incremental] [--dry-run]
                                 # print the sweep plan (sessions past retention, zero-ref content rows, ~pages reclaimable), then run the same gc() the HTTP endpoint calls; --dry-run stops after the plan

// require the unified store (BILI_STORAGE_UNIFIED=shadow|full or in the config file) — legacy-only installs refuse with a hint. defaults to (365). No scheduler: these run on demand. All commands accept .

Full vacuum is an offline operation on large databases (#4612). (the default) rewrites the entire index.db under an exclusive write lock — O(db size), minutes to tens of minutes on multi-GB databases, with no intermediate progress (SQLite's VACUUM is atomic; it cannot be split). Running it while a proxy is serving from the same sessions dir starves that proxy's writes until its storage layer degrades, so refuses to start when another live process holds the database ( pid discipline, #4175): the CLI exits 1 with an actionable message, the panel endpoint returns HTTP 409. Stop the other instance first (or wait for it to exit) and retry; for online-safe shrink use , which reclaims freed pages in short transactions without taking the exclusive lock. The zero-ref delete sweep itself is batched with per-batch progress output either way.

Early. Protocol handling and compression work against mock tests (500+ passing). Real-model integration testing is the next milestone. Expect rough edges.

Client-side plugins for pi / omp / opencode ship inside () for the cooperative-proxy path. See the section above for how , the standalone , and relate.

Attribution requirement (one term on top of MIT)

This project is MIT-licensed : any product or service (commercial or open source) whose users can see or interact with it and which uses this software must attribute it — stating that it uses billion-context with a link back to this repository — on its home page, documentation, or About/Credits page. Pure server-side/embedded use satisfies this via shipped documentation. See the at the end of LICENSE.

If you build on this project, we'd love to hear about it: open an issue (no obligation) so we can track where it's used.

items.title: mbillow/localthings
items.content:
Control your Samsung appliances from Home Assistant over your home network, with no cloud account.

Control your Samsung appliances from Home Assistant over your home network, with no cloud account.

LocalThings connects Home Assistant to Samsung washers, dryers, refrigerators, air conditioners, ovens and other appliances that work with the SmartThings app. It talks to each appliance on your local network.

  • Appliances that support push send changes as they happen. LocalThings checks the rest every 30 seconds.
  • It works without the internet. After setup, LocalThings never contacts Samsung's servers.
  • LocalThings sends nothing to Samsung. The appliance itself still keeps its own connection to Samsung, and LocalThings doesn't change that.
  • Setup needs an IP address. For most appliances, you enter the address and LocalThings works out the type and model, then creates matching controls and sensors.
Air conditioner, including multi-unit systems
Refrigerator, kimchi refrigerator, wine cellar
Cooktop, gas, radiant electric and induction; some models read-onlyRobot vacuum, early support
Soundbar, media player, settings and status

What you see depends on what each appliance reports. Typical controls and sensors include power, program or mode selection, start, pause and stop, temperatures and setpoints, time remaining and finish time, door and child-lock state, energy use, filter status and alarms.

Most Samsung appliances from about 2022 onward work, and so do some earlier washers, air conditioners and wall ovens that use an older local interface. See Older appliances on TCP 8888. Setup detects which interface an appliance has, and tells you if it finds none.

If an appliance sets up but LocalThings doesn't recognize it, or a control is missing, Home Assistant shows a notice asking for a diagnostics download. That download is usually all the maintainers need to add support. See Reporting a capability gap.

LocalThings uses the standards the appliances implement:

  • Samsung's connected appliances are OCF devices. LocalThings discovers each appliance's resources through and reads its device type, such as , from . Where an appliance offers both a standard OCF resource and a Samsung extension for the same state, LocalThings uses the standard one.
  • LocalThings sends Constrained Application Protocol requests, defined in RFC 7252, over an encrypted DTLS session with an X.509 client certificate. It uses CoAP Observe, RFC 7641, for push updates, and block-wise transfer, RFC 7959, for large responses. The library implements the protocol layer.
  • Home Assistant's own patterns. Setup, reconfigure and reauthentication run in the UI config flow. A data-update coordinator combines push and polling. DHCP discovery follows an appliance to a new IP address. Repairs notices report gaps. LocalThings redacts diagnostics downloads and translates entity names into twelve languages.
  • Declarative appliance maps. Each appliance type is a table that maps the resources an appliance reports to Home Assistant entities. Tests check the tables against 90+ captures from real appliances, so a new model usually needs a table entry and no protocol code.

  1. In HACS, go to , search for , and select . LocalThings is in HACS's default list, so you don't need to add a custom repository.

    Without HACS, copy custom_components/localthings/ into the folder of your Home Assistant config.

  1. Go to Settings > Devices & Services > Add Integration > LocalThings.
  2. Enter the appliance's IP address. For most appliances, that's the whole setup.
  3. LocalThings connects, reads the appliance's type and model, and adds one Home Assistant device for it.

When you add your first appliance, LocalThings contacts Samsung's servers once to read a public identifier. It uses no account or login. Later appliances reuse that identifier, so adding them needs only an IP address and no internet access.

A few appliances need one more step:

  • Some appliances refuse the automatic certificate. Setup then offers to import a pre-shared key, which LocalThings can't obtain for you. Credential acquisition covers where one comes from. We're still working to understand these appliances, and #435 has the plan, what we've found so far, and a place to report how it went. Setup also offers the public CA certificate, which the project's shows how to get, but no appliance that refused the automatic certificate has been reported to accept it.

You can rename devices. LocalThings identifies each appliance by its OCF device ID, not by its name or serial number. Some models ship the same serial number on every unit.

Each appliance has a option in Settings > Devices & Services, with these settings under :

  • "Allow writes even when remote control is reported off". By default, LocalThings refuses a command while the appliance reports remote control off, and shows an error, because the appliance would ignore the command without saying so. Some appliances accept certain commands anyway. Turn this on only after you confirm yours does.
  • "Estimated finish -- minimum change (minutes)". LocalThings holds a washer's, dryer's or dishwasher's finish time until the appliance's estimate changes by at least this many minutes. This keeps one-minute jitter out of your history. The default is 3. Set 0 to report every change.
  • "Remember modes the device reports but doesn't advertise". Some appliances run in a mode they never list as available. With this setting on, which is the default, LocalThings remembers such a mode and keeps offering it. in the same menu clears the list.

An appliance that exposes more than one device, such as each indoor unit of a multi-split system or each cavity of a dual oven, also gets in the same menu. Some appliances report an extra slot that isn't real hardware, which shows up as a duplicate or empty device. Untick it there: LocalThings removes that device and stops reading it. Tick it again to bring it back.

Brief disconnects are normal. Samsung appliances drop their connection for a moment now and then. LocalThings reconnects, and entities keep their last value meanwhile. If reconnects happen several times a minute, check the appliance's Wi-Fi signal. Also check that nothing else on your network holds a connection to it, because an appliance accepts one connection at a time.

Keep appliances registered in SmartThings. If you remove an appliance from SmartThings, it resets its network settings the next time it reaches Samsung's servers. It then drops off Wi-Fi until you set it up in the app again. This happens even if you block its internet access most of the time.

Some washers and dryers stop counting energy without SmartThings. On the DA_WM_TP2_20_COMMON board (for example the WW80T654ALX and DV80T6220LX), the energy total stops increasing while the appliance can't reach SmartThings, and resumes once it reconnects. LocalThings can only show what the appliance records, so if your energy sensor stays at one value while cycles run, check that the appliance can reach Samsung's servers.

Restarting while an appliance is powered off

If Home Assistant restarts while an appliance is off, LocalThings loads the appliance's device and entities from the last successful setup. They show until the appliance answers, then recover without any action from you. This works for any appliance LocalThings has reached at least once. A new appliance must be reachable to set it up.

When an appliance's IP address changes

About half of Samsung's appliances report their Wi-Fi MAC address. For those, Home Assistant's DHCP discovery spots the new address and LocalThings updates the entry. For other appliances, select on the entry and enter the new address. LocalThings checks that the appliance at that address is the right one, and keeps its entities, history and automations. Deleting and re-adding the appliance would lose all three.

Older appliances on TCP 8888

Some appliances from about 2018 to 2022 have a different local interface, HTTPS on TCP port 8888. So far this covers a WW6500 washer, TP6X air conditioners, an NV51K777OS Flex Duo wall oven, an NQ70M6650DS microwave/oven combo, NZ36K7570R and NZ30K7570RS cooktops, and an RF28K9380SR refrigerator. Setup detects the interface from the IP address and then asks for a . Leave the field empty and the appliance issues a token, sending it back to Home Assistant on port 8889. For that to work, switch Remote Control on at the appliance with the door closed, and make sure the appliance can reach Home Assistant on port 8889. If the appliance later rejects its token, Home Assistant asks for a new one.

On the RF28K9380SR refrigerator, when setup asks for the token, hold for about 5 seconds, until "on" shows in the freezer temperature display. It refuses the automatic certificate, so setup then asks for an AC14K_M CA certificate and key, and it needs both to finish.

For the tested NZ36K7570R and NZ30K7570RS cooktops, NV51K777OS oven and NQ70M6650DS combo, if Smart Connect is already on, no token will be returned. Turn it off, request a token in LocalThings, then turn it on.

On these appliances, a chosen cycle, temperature, rinse count or spin speed takes effect only when the cycle starts. The selects hold your choice, and the button sends it. If you turn the dial on the appliance, the dial's setting replaces the held choice.

This interface speaks only TLS 1.0 and presents a certificate LocalThings can't verify, so LocalThings accepts both on this one connection. No other part of LocalThings relaxes TLS.

Starting an oven, range or microwave

An oven only starts when the mode, temperature and cook time arrive together. While it's idle, the mode select, setpoint and cook time hold your choice, starting from the mode's own defaults, and the button sends them. The localthings.start_cooking action does the same in one call, with any value you leave out taken from the mode's defaults. Once a cook is running, changes to the setpoint and cook time go straight to the oven.

Each appliance reports which of its modes a remote may start, and the temperature and time limits for each. LocalThings follows that list, and only offers the modes the oven can run right now. The button appears only on an appliance that reports at least one mode it can start, and a start outside those limits is refused with the allowed range. On a range with two ovens, each oven has its own Start cooking button and starts separately. Some modes can't be started remotely by design: on every microwave seen so far, none of the microwave-power modes can be. Remote Control has to be on at the appliance, and it switches off after a power cut.

Multi-unit air conditioners

Some installations run several indoor units from one outdoor unit, all at one IP address. LocalThings finds the extra units after its first connection. Each unit gets its own Home Assistant device and climate card, linked to the main unit. LocalThings skips the unused slots some systems report. If a unit you expect is missing, attach a diagnostics download to an issue.

Reporting a capability gap

If LocalThings doesn't recognize an appliance, or the appliance reports something LocalThings doesn't handle yet, a notice appears under Settings > System > Repairs. It points you to on the device. LocalThings removes personal and network details from that download before you save it. It removes the account email, tokens, device IDs, MAC addresses, serial numbers, the Wi-Fi network name and password, the device's name, the name of a paired phone and the device's on/off history. You can attach the file to a device-support issue, and that is the fastest way to get an appliance supported.

A diagnostics download can't show whether a command sticks or what order commands need. The localthings.read_resource and localthings.write_resource actions answer those questions by reading and writing an appliance's resources without going through its entities. See Reading and writing resources directly.

We welcome patches, especially:

  • Support for appliance types LocalThings doesn't cover yet, or for models that don't fully work. Start from a diagnostics download. CONTRIBUTING.md covers adding a type.
  • Reports that confirm or rule out more models of a supported type.
  • Protocol-level fixes. These belong upstream in . Fixes to entities, setup, the coordinator or the registry belong here.

Please don't include real device UUIDs, MAC addresses, serial numbers, IP addresses or private keys in a pull request. CONTRIBUTING.md covers the dev environment, the checks to run, the repo layout, and the rules for comments and commits.

Hunt down social media accounts by username across social networks

Packages for ParrotOS and Ubuntu 24.04, maintained by a third party, appear to be . Users of these systems should defer to // or Docker.

pipx install sherlock-project or may be used in place of
docker run -it --rm sherlock/sherlock

Community-maintained packages are available for Debian (>= 13), Ubuntu (>= 22.10), Homebrew, Kali, and BlackArch. These packages are not directly supported or maintained by the Sherlock Project.

See all alternative installation methods here.

To search for only one user:

To search for more than one user:

sherlock user1 user2 user3

Accounts found will be stored in an individual text file with the corresponding username (e.g ).

$ sherlock --help
usage: sherlock [-h] [--version] [--verbose] [--folderoutput FOLDEROUTPUT] [--output OUTPUT] [--csv] [--xlsx] [--site SITE_NAME] [--proxy PROXY_URL] [--dump-response]
                [--json JSON_FILE] [--timeout TIMEOUT] [--print-all] [--print-found] [--no-color] [--browse] [--local] [--nsfw] [--txt] [--ignore-exclusions]
                USERNAMES [USERNAMES ...]

Sherlock: Find Usernames Across Social Networks (Version 0.16.0)

positional arguments:
  USERNAMES             One or more usernames to check with social networks. Check similar usernames using {?} (replace to '_', '-', '.').

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --version             Display version information and dependencies.
  --verbose, -v, -d, --debug
                        Display extra debugging information and metrics.
  --folderoutput FOLDEROUTPUT, -fo FOLDEROUTPUT
                        If using multiple usernames, the output of the results will be saved to this folder.
  --output OUTPUT, -o OUTPUT
                        If using single username, the output of the result will be saved to this file.
  --csv                 Create Comma-Separated Values (CSV) File.
  --xlsx                Create the standard file for the modern Microsoft Excel spreadsheet (xlsx).
  --site SITE_NAME      Limit analysis to just the listed sites. Add multiple options to specify more than one site.

                        Make requests over a proxy. e.g. socks5://127.0.0.1:1080
  --dump-response       Dump the HTTP response to stdout for targeted debugging.

                        Load data from a JSON file or an online, valid, JSON file. Upstream PR numbers also accepted.

  --print-found         Output sites where the username was found (also if exported as file).

items.title: meta/astryx
items.content:
An open source design system that's fully customizable and agent ready

Astryx is an open source design system that grew inside Meta over the last eight years, where it became the most-used and largest design system in the company — powering 13,000+ apps and shaped by the engineers, designers, and product teams who depend on it every day.

It ships 150+ accessible components, brand-level theming, dark mode, ready-to-ship templates, and a CLI as one cohesive system. You import pre-built CSS and use typed React components — no build plugin, no styling library to adopt — and both people and AI assistants build with the same tooling.

What makes Astryx different:

  • Components are built to be composed at any level, not locked behind a closed top-level API. The building blocks you'd reach for are exported directly, and when you need to go deeper, swizzle ejects a component's full source into your project to own.
  • Astryx authors its styles with StyleX, but that's invisible to consumers. Override with using Tailwind, CSS modules, or plain CSS — whatever your project already uses.
  • Customize without wrapping. A theme is a set of CSS custom property overrides, so a designer can make Astryx unmistakably theirs without forking or wrapping component source.
  • Built for people and agents. The API, docs, and CLI are designed together so a person and an AI assistant build the same way, from the same reference.

Astryx requires or later ( and are peer dependencies of ).

Install Astryx, a theme, and its peer dependencies:

# npm
npm install @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
npm install -D @astryxdesign/cli

# pnpm
pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
pnpm add -D @astryxdesign/cli

# yarn
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @stylexjs/stylex
yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli

You can also install the CLI once for your computer, so works in any folder and every coding agent knows Astryx; in a project, it still runs that project's own version:

npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli

Project install, global install, or both? astryx docs global/project-global-or-both compares them (both is recommended), and explains how global mode works.

The simplest setup is a few CSS imports plus a theme provider — no build plugin, no PostCSS or Babel config. See the for the full guide (Next.js, Tailwind, Vite, and CDN).

For reliable CLI access, add a script to your :

"scripts": {
  "astryx": "node node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/clients/cli/bin/astryx.mjs"
}

Then use it as npm run astryx -- component --list. This avoids path errors when AI assistants or new developers invoke the CLI directly.

(experimental components) is used internally for Storybook and the sandbox and is not published to npm. (Vega/Vega-Lite chart wrapper) and (chart components) are published to npm only under the dist-tag — there is no stable release yet.

These are the promises Astryx makes to the people building on it.

  • Guidance over enforcement. Components give you capability rather than guardrails that fight you. Design opinions live in docs and examples — if you pass a value, the component renders it.
  • Strong, documented conventions. Every component follows the same naming, prop, and composition rules, and every one is thoroughly documented — so once you've learned a few, the rest feel familiar, and both people and AI can predict how an unfamiliar component behaves.
  • One system for humans and AI. The API, conventions, docs, and CLI are designed together so people and AI assistants build the same way. Every change that made Astryx easier for AI made it easier for people too.
  • We test conventions rather than assert them, hold the results loosely, and revisit them when a new situation proves them wrong.

The building blocks for visually cohesive and accessible interfaces: typography, color, layout, and accessibility.

A library of 150+ reusable UI building blocks with full TypeScript support.

Battle-tested design solutions for common interactions and workflows: table pages, detail page layouts, form wizards, navigation patterns, data entry flows.

Example apps, the docsite, and Storybook
Published packages: core, cli, build, themes
Internal tooling: test utilities, eslint plugin, vibe tests

Questions, or want a hand with a PR? Come find us in .

Quick start for contributors: this repo uses Node 22+ on an active LTS line and . Install pnpm directly, or enable Corepack once so the pinned pnpm version installs automatically:

corepack enable
pnpm install

If is missing, install pnpm directly or install Corepack manually; see the troubleshooting notes in CONTRIBUTING.md.

The Theme Showcase DOM tests use the root project for shared DOM and StyleX test setup. Run pnpm exec vitest run --project ui apps/docsite/src/__tests__/theme-showcase/ from the repository root.

items.title: astral-sh/ruff
items.content:
An extremely fast Python linter and code formatter, written in Rust.

An extremely fast Python linter and code formatter, written in Rust.

Linting the CPython codebase from scratch.

  • ⚡️ 10-100x faster than existing linters (like Flake8) and formatters (like Black)
  • 🤝 Python 3.15 compatibility
  • 📦 Built-in caching, to avoid re-analyzing unchanged files
  • 🔧 Fix support, for automatic error correction (e.g., automatically remove unused imports)
  • 📏 Over 900 built-in rules, with native re-implementations of popular Flake8 plugins, like flake8-bugbear

Ruff aims to be orders of magnitude faster than alternative tools while integrating more functionality behind a single, common interface.

Ruff is actively developed and used in major open-source projects like:

Ruff is so fast that sometimes I add an intentional bug in the code just to confirm it's actually running and checking the code.

Why is Ruff a gamechanger? Primarily because it is nearly 1000x faster. Literally. Not a typo. On our largest module (dagster itself, 250k LOC) pylint takes about 2.5 minutes, parallelized across 4 cores on my M1. Running ruff against our codebase takes .4 seconds.

Ruff is ~150-200x faster than flake8 on my machine, scanning the whole repo takes ~0.2s instead of ~20s. This is an enormous quality of life improvement for local dev. It's fast enough that I added it as an actual commit hook, which is terrific.

Just switched my first project to Ruff. Only one downside so far: it's so fast I couldn't believe it was working till I intentionally introduced some errors.

This is just ridiculously fast... is amazing.

Ruff is available as on PyPI.

Invoke Ruff directly with :

uvx ruff@0.17.4 check   # Lint all files in the current directory.
uvx ruff@0.17.4 format  # Format all files in the current directory.

Or install Ruff with (recommended), , or :

# With uv.
uv tool install ruff@latest  # Install Ruff globally.
uv add --dev ruff            # Or add Ruff to your project.

# With pip.
pip install ruff

# With pipx.
pipx install ruff

Starting with version , Ruff can be installed with our standalone installers:

# On macOS and Linux.
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/ruff/install.sh | sh

# On Windows.
powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/ruff/install.ps1 | iex"

# For a specific version.
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/ruff/0.17.4/install.sh | sh
powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/ruff/0.17.4/install.ps1 | iex"

To run Ruff as a linter, try any of the following:

ruff check                          # Lint all files in the current directory (and any subdirectories).
ruff check path/to/code/            # Lint all files in `/path/to/code` (and any subdirectories).
ruff check path/to/code/*.py        # Lint all `.py` files in `/path/to/code`.
ruff check path/to/code/to/file.py  # Lint `file.py`.
ruff check @arguments.txt           # Lint using an input file, treating its contents as newline-delimited command-line arguments.

Or, to run Ruff as a formatter:

ruff format                          # Format all files in the current directory (and any subdirectories).
ruff format path/to/code/            # Format all files in `/path/to/code` (and any subdirectories).
ruff format path/to/code/*.py        # Format all `.py` files in `/path/to/code`.
ruff format path/to/code/to/file.py  # Format `file.py`.
ruff format @arguments.txt           # Format using an input file, treating its contents as newline-delimited command-line arguments.

- repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
  # Ruff version.
  rev: v0.17.4
  hooks:
    # Run the linter.
    - id: ruff-check
      args: [ --fix ]
    # Run the formatter.
    - id: ruff-format

name: Ruff
on: [ push, pull_request ]
jobs:
  ruff:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/ruff-action@v3

Ruff can be configured through a , , or file (see: , or for a complete list of all configuration options).

If left unspecified, Ruff's default configuration is equivalent to the following file:

# Exclude a variety of commonly ignored directories.
exclude = [
    ".bzr",
    ".direnv",
    ".eggs",
    ".git",
    ".git-rewrite",
    ".hg",
    ".ipynb_checkpoints",
    ".mypy_cache",
    ".nox",
    ".pants.d",
    ".pyenv",
    ".pytest_cache",
    ".pytype",
    ".ruff_cache",
    ".svn",
    ".tox",
    ".venv",
    ".vscode",
    "__pypackages__",
    "_build",
    "buck-out",
    "build",
    "dist",
    "node_modules",
    "site-packages",
    "venv",
]

# Same as Black.
line-length = 88
indent-width = 4

# Assume Python 3.11
target-version = "py311"

[lint]
# select = [...]  # See the Default Rules page for the full listing.
ignore = []

# Allow fix for all enabled rules (when `--fix`) is provided.
fixable = ["ALL"]
unfixable = []

# Allow unused variables when underscore-prefixed.
dummy-variable-rgx = "^(_+|(_+[\\p{XID_Continue}]*[\\p{XID_Continue}--_]+?))$"

[format]
# Like Black, use double quotes for strings.
quote-style = "double"

# Like Black, indent with spaces, rather than tabs.
indent-style = "space"

# Like Black, respect magic trailing commas.
skip-magic-trailing-comma = false

# Like Black, automatically detect the appropriate line ending.
line-ending = "auto"

Note that, in a , each section header should be prefixed with . For example, should be replaced with .

Some configuration options can be provided via dedicated command-line arguments, such as those related to rule enablement and disablement, file discovery, and logging level:

ruff check --select F401 --select F403 --quiet

The remaining configuration options can be provided through a catch-all argument:

ruff check --config "lint.per-file-ignores = {'some_file.py' = ['F841']}"

To opt in to the latest lint rules, formatter style changes, interface updates, and more, enable preview mode by setting in your configuration file or passing on the command line. Preview mode enables a collection of unstable features that may change prior to stabilization.

See for more on Ruff's top-level commands, or and for more on the linting and formatting commands, respectively.

Ruff supports over 900 lint rules, many of which are inspired by popular tools like Flake8, isort, pyupgrade, and others. Regardless of the rule's origin, Ruff re-implements every rule in Rust as a first-party feature.

By default, Ruff enables rules from the , , , , and categories, as well as many more, omitting any stylistic rules that overlap with the use of a formatter, like or Black.

If you're just getting started with Ruff, the default rule set is a great place to start: it catches a wide variety of common errors (like unused imports) with zero configuration. See for the complete list.

Beyond the defaults, Ruff re-implements some of the most popular Flake8 plugins and related code quality tools, including:

For the complete list of supported rules, see .

You can also ask for help on .

In some cases, Ruff includes a "direct" Rust port of the corresponding tool. We're grateful to the maintainers of these tools for their work, and for all the value they've provided to the Python community.

Ruff's import resolver is based on the import resolution algorithm from Pyright.

Ruff is also influenced by a number of tools outside the Python ecosystem, like Clippy and ESLint.

Ruff is released under the MIT license.

If you're using Ruff, consider adding the Ruff badge to your project's :

[![Ruff](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json)](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff)

.. image:: https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json
    :target: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff
    :alt: Ruff

<a href="https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff"><img src="https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json" alt="Ruff" style="max-width:100%;"></a>

items.title: cloudflare/security-audit-skill
items.content:
A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings

A coding-agent skill that turns your agent into a security auditor. It orchestrates isolated agents through reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting.

This is the skill that seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness, described in Build your own vulnerability harness. The harness grew into a multi-stage, fleet-wide system; this skill is the single-repo starting point it evolved from.

The skill runs a structured audit in six phases:

  1. -- map architecture, trust boundaries, input surfaces, prior evidence, and deterministic coverage in and .
  2. -- assign isolated hunters from ledger units, record their checks, and use coverage critics to find gaps.
  3. -- give every unique candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it.
  4. -- write , , and records to and validate them against .
  5. Independent record verification -- fresh agents verify final source claims. Material replacements receive another independent verifier.
  6. -- derive , , and from the verified records and coverage ledger.

The parent runs validate-coverage-ledger.cjs after creating the ledger and after each later ledger update. It runs in Phase 4 and again after every Phase 5 replacement.

The verdicts are distinct: has a complete source trace and bounded observed result, has an exact unresolved fact and no severity, and records a disproved candidate.

Multiple runs against the same repo are additive. The skill uses prior ledgers and findings to target gaps, revalidate changed source, and carry forward current-source evidence without treating stale or unresolved work as covered.

Setup, core principles, platform terminology, workflow overview, and audit anti-patterns
Phase 1 reconnaissance prompts and synthesis instructions
Phase 2 orchestration, hunting methodology, and validation rules
Core, wildcard, and obvious-things attack prompts
MEMORY-SAFETY-AND-BINARY.mdMemory-safety, binary, and kernel hunting classes for native targets
Prompt-injection, agent/tool, and output-handling hunting classes for LLM-backed targets
HTTP request-framing, cache, and authentication-protocol hunting classes for HTTP-protocol and auth targets
DOM-injection, messaging-trust, UI-redress, and prototype-pollution hunting classes for client-side/browser targets
SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.mdDependency, CI, release, signing, update, plugin, and extension hunting classes
IAM, infrastructure-as-code, container, serverless, ingress, and runtime-configuration hunting classes
PROTOCOLS-RPC-AND-MESSAGING.mdRPC, serialization, queue, broker, webhook, and streaming-protocol hunting classes
RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY.mdShared resource, quota, queue, worker, and operator-spend hunting classes
DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.mdTenant isolation, cache, search, export, backup, migration, deletion, and restore hunting classes
DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.mdNative app, deep-link, webview, exported-component, helper, daemon, and local-IPC hunting classes
VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.mdPhases 3–6 candidate validation, structured output, record verification, and reporting
JSON schema for all three verdicts
Zero-dependency validator for in Phases 4 and 5
validate-findings.test.cjsFindings-validator tests and producer-compatible fixture checks
validate-coverage-ledger.cjsZero-dependency validator for in Phases 1–5
validate-coverage-ledger.test.cjsCoverage-ledger validator tests
npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit

Use for a user-level installation:

npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit \
  --global

Run for agent-selection and non-interactive options.

Start your coding agent in (or pointed at) the codebase you want to audit, then ask it to do a security audit:

security audit this codebase

find security vulnerabilities in ./src

do a security review, output to ~/audits/my-project

The skill activates automatically when the request matches its trigger (security audit, find vulnerabilities, pen-test the code, etc.). A direct codebase audit or pen-test request uses full audit mode. Security questions and focused vulnerability work use guidance mode unless you request report artifacts. In full audit mode, an unspecified output directory defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>. The workflow writes inside the target repository only when you explicitly select a directory that version control ignores.

  • A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents
  • Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators
  • An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as instead of executing target code.
  • Only confirm established boundary failures. Keep a source-grounded blocked lead as with its exact unresolved fact.
  • The agent that checks a finding is never the agent that found it.
  • Severity requires impact. Likelihood x impact, not deviation from a checklist.
  • Defense-in-depth gaps are not vulnerabilities. If Layer A prevents the attack, the absence of Layer B is a hardening note.
  • Multiple runs improve coverage. In our test runs, a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total.

items.title: openssl/openssl
items.content:
General purpose TLS and crypto library

OpenSSL is a robust, commercial-grade, full-featured Open Source Toolkit for the Transport Layer Security (TLS, formerly SSL), Datagram TLS (DTLS), and QUIC protocols.

The protocol implementations are based on a full-strength general purpose cryptographic library, which can also be used stand-alone. Also included is a cryptographic module validated to conform with FIPS standards.

OpenSSL is descended from the SSLeay library developed by Eric A. Young and Tim J. Hudson.

The OpenSSL toolkit includes:

  • an implementation of all TLS protocol versions up to TLSv1.3 (RFC 8446), DTLS protocol versions up to DTLSv1.3 (RFC 9147) and the QUIC version 1 protocol (RFC 9000).

  • a full-strength general purpose cryptographic library. It constitutes the basis of the TLS implementation, but can also be used independently.

  • the OpenSSL command line tool, a Swiss Army knife for cryptographic tasks, testing and analyzing. It can be used for

    • creation of key parameters
    • creation of X.509 certificates, CSRs and CRLs
    • calculation of message digests
    • encryption and decryption
    • SSL/TLS/DTLS and client and server tests
    • handling of S/MIME signed or encrypted mail

Source code tarballs of the official releases can be downloaded from openssl-library.org/source/. The OpenSSL project does not distribute the toolkit in binary form.

However, for a large variety of operating systems precompiled versions of the OpenSSL toolkit are available. In particular, on Linux and other Unix operating systems, it is normally recommended to link against the precompiled shared libraries provided by the distributor or vendor.

We also maintain a list of third parties that produce OpenSSL binaries for various Operating Systems (including Windows) on the Binaries page on our wiki.

For Testing and Development

Although testing and development could in theory also be done using the source tarballs, having a local copy of the git repository with the entire project history gives you much more insight into the code base.

The main OpenSSL Git repository is private. There is a public GitHub mirror of it at github.com/openssl/openssl, which is updated automatically from the former on every commit.

A local copy of the Git repository can be obtained by cloning it from the GitHub mirror using

git clone https://github.com/openssl/openssl.git

If you intend to contribute to OpenSSL, either to fix bugs or contribute new features, you need to fork the GitHub mirror and clone your public fork instead.

git clone https://github.com/yourname/openssl.git

This is necessary because all development of OpenSSL nowadays is done via GitHub pull requests. For more details, see Contributing.

After obtaining the Source, have a look at the INSTALL file for detailed instructions about building and installing OpenSSL. For some platforms, the installation instructions are amended by a platform specific document.

There are some README.md files in the top level of the source distribution containing additional information on specific topics.

There are some tutorial and introductory pages on some important OpenSSL topics within the OpenSSL Guide.

The manual pages for the master branch and all current stable releases are available online.

There are numerous source code demos for using various OpenSSL capabilities in the demos subfolder.

There is a GitHub Wiki which is currently not very active.

OpenSSL is licensed under the Apache License 2.0, which means that you are free to get and use it for commercial and non-commercial purposes as long as you fulfill its conditions.

There are various ways to get in touch. The correct channel depends on your requirement. See the SUPPORT file for more details.

If you are interested and willing to contribute to the OpenSSL project, please take a look at the CONTRIBUTING file.

A number of nations restrict the use or export of cryptography. If you are potentially subject to such restrictions, you should seek legal advice before attempting to develop or distribute cryptographic code.

Copyright (c) 1998-2026 The OpenSSL Project Authors

Copyright (c) 1995-1998 Eric A. Young, Tim J. Hudson

etcd is written in Go and uses the Raft consensus algorithm to manage a highly-available replicated log.

The most common API documentation you'll need can be found here:

Maintainers strive to shape an inclusive open source project culture where users are heard and contributors feel respected and empowered. Maintainers aim to build productive relationships across different companies and disciplines. Read more about Maintainers role and responsibilities.

/tmp/etcd-download-test/etcd
